notes.title: The operating rhythm: maker vs manager time
notes.body:
Senior analysts protect deep-work blocks (analysis, modeling) while serving stakeholder time (meetings, ad-hoc). The rhythm: mornings for deep work, afternoons for collaboration, Friday for pipeline health and learning. Context-switching is the tax; batching is the deduction.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sample senior-analyst week:
Mon AM: deep work (the hard analysis) | PM: stakeholder meetings
Tue AM: deep work | PM: pipeline review + code reviews
Wed AM: deep work | PM: metric review prep
Thu: metric review meeting + follow-up analyses
Fri AM: pipeline health + break inventory | PM: learning (new technique)
Rules: no-meeting mornings twice a week (calendar-blocked); ad-hoc requests
triaged, not instantly served ('I'll scope it by 3pm'); the metric review
is sacred (it's where trust compounds).
```

notes.title: The daily/weekly/monthly cadence
notes.body:
Daily: pipeline health check (did everything run? any breaks?), inbox triage, one deep-work block. Weekly: metric review, stakeholder updates, pipeline break inventory. Monthly: deep-dives, roadmap planning, skill investment. The cadence turns chaos into routine.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Daily 15-minute pipeline check:
1. Orchestrator: all DAGs green? (if red: which task, what error)
2. Freshness: max(event_time) within SLA on critical tables?
3. Quality gates: any failed checks overnight?
4. Dashboard subscriptions: any delivery failures?
Log it (even 'all green'): the log is the evidence when someone asks
'when did this break?' Silence in the log means 'I wasn't watching.'
```

notes.title: Incident playbook: the dashboard is wrong
notes.body:
Production incidents follow a playbook: acknowledge quickly, assess impact (who sees wrong numbers?), diagnose at pipeline boundaries, communicate status, fix forward, then write the blameless postmortem. Never fix forward silently — the postmortem is where the system improves.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
09:12 Alert: exec dashboard revenue down 40%.
09:15 Acknowledge in #data-ops: 'Investigating; dashboard may show stale data.'
09:25 Diagnose: mart_daily partition for yesterday is EMPTY (load failed at 03:00).
09:30 Communicate: 'Root cause: failed load; rerunning now; ETA 10:30.'
10:25 Rerun completes; quality gates pass; dashboard correct.
10:45 Postmortem: why did the load fail (source schema change)? Add a schema-
drift check as a gate. Action item with owner and date.
Calm, structured, communicative: the senior incident signature.
```

notes.title: Stakeholder portfolio: managing up, down, and across
notes.body:
Senior analysts manage a stakeholder portfolio: executives (decisions, brevity), peers in data eng (contracts, respect), business partners (discovery, reliability), and finance (tie-outs, rigor). Each gets a different cadence and format; all get reliability.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Stakeholder map:
- VP Product: monthly metric review, one-slide decisions, 60-second answers.
- Data Eng: DAG contracts, schema-change notices, blameless postmortems.
- Marketing: weekly office hours (batches ad-hoc into one slot).
- Finance: tie-out packages, variance bridges, audit-ready docs.
The office-hours trick: ad-hoc requests arrive all week but get ANSWERED
in the slot — batching protects deep work while serving partners well.
```

notes.title: Growth: feedback, skills, and compounding habits
notes.body:
Senior growth is deliberate: quarterly feedback (ask 'what should I do more/less of?'), skill investment (one new technique per quarter, applied to real work), teaching (the fastest way to learn), and a portfolio habit (one public artifact per quarter). Careers compound like interest.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Quarterly growth plan:
- Feedback: ask manager + 2 stakeholders the more/less question; write it down.
- Skill: this quarter = dbt testing; apply to the team's marts (real work).
- Teaching: run a 30-min lunch-and-learn on window functions.
- Portfolio: publish the dbt-testing writeup (sanitized) as a blog post.
Each quarter's artifact becomes next quarter's interview story.
The analysts who compound: visible learning, applied immediately, taught
to others, published. That loop is the career.
```

notes.title: The 7-project architecture
notes.body:
Seven projects, each proving a hiring-relevant skill: (1) SQL deep-dive (window functions, CTEs on a real dataset), (2) pandas analysis (wrangling + EDA), (3) statistics/A/B test (experiment analysis with memo), (4) dashboard (BI tool, takeaway-first), (5) Excel model (forecast with checks), (6) domain project (banking/healthcare/retail data story), (7) capstone (end-to-end: question to stakeholder deck). No toy datasets — real, messy, documented.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Project scoping template (fill BEFORE building):
Decision question: 'Should we expand the loyalty program?'
Dataset: e-commerce orders + loyalty table (source + grain documented).
Methods: cohort retention, CAC comparison, Simpson check by tenure.
Deliverable: one-slide recommendation + notebook + dashboard.
Done when: a stranger can reproduce it from the README in 30 minutes.
Build order: SQL (fastest win) -> pandas -> dashboard -> A/B -> Excel ->
domain -> capstone. Early wins fund later motivation.
```

notes.title: What hiring managers actually look for
notes.body:
Hiring managers skim portfolios in minutes. They check: can this person frame a question, handle messiness, choose right methods, communicate a takeaway, and write clean code? They do NOT check: tutorial completion, perfect accuracy, fancy tools. Signal density beats project count.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
90-second README structure (every project):
# Title: the decision question (not 'Sales Analysis')
> One-line takeaway: 'Churn concentrates in month 2; onboarding is the leak.'
## The question | ## Data (source, grain, caveats) | ## Method (3 bullets)
## Key visual (one chart) | ## Recommendation | ## Reproduce (commands)
The hiring manager reads the title + takeaway + visual in 90 seconds
and decides 'interview' or 'pass'. Everything else is for the deep read.
```

notes.title: Real datasets, honestly documented
notes.body:
Use public real datasets (government open data, Kaggle with documented provenance, company-released data) — never fabricate 'real company' data. Document every caveat: sampling, time range, known gaps. Honest limitations are a senior signal; hidden ones are a rejection.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Dataset documentation block (README):
Source: NYC Open Data, taxi trips 2026-01 (link + access date).
Grain: one row per trip. Rows: 2.1M.
Caveats: cash tips underreported; GPS rounding at pickup; Jan only
(seasonality not observable).
License: public domain.
Why this matters: the interviewer WILL ask 'what are this data's limits?'
The documented answer beats the improvised one every time.
```

notes.title: Code quality that survives skimming
notes.body:
Portfolio code is read, not run: clear names, short functions, comments explaining WHY (not what), a requirements file, and deterministic outputs (seeds set). Notebooks: narrative + code, executed top-to-bottom with no hidden state.

Worked example (with solution):
```python
# Bad: df2 = df[df.x > 5].groupby('y').z.mean()  (what is df2? why 5?)
# Good:
MIN_ORDERS = 5  # filter noise: customers with fewer orders
avg_value_by_segment = (
    customers[customers['orders'] >= MIN_ORDERS]
    .groupby('segment')['lifetime_value'].mean()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)
# Names say what; the comment says why (filtering noise).
# requirements.txt pins pandas==2.x; random_state=42 everywhere.
```

notes.title: The capstone: end-to-end proof
notes.body:
Project 7 ties everything: a real decision question, raw data, cleaning, SQL + Python analysis, statistics, a dashboard, and a stakeholder deck. It is the interview centerpiece — the story you walk through for 10 minutes while they probe every choice.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Capstone arc (10-minute walkthrough):
0:00 'The question: should the company expand loyalty?' (decision)
2:00 'Data: 3 tables, grain documented; the loyalty table had 12% dup keys
      (fixed via dedup, documented).' (messiness handled)
4:00 'Method: cohort retention + CAC math + Simpson check.' (rigor)
6:00 'Finding: 2x retention concentrates in tenured users; marginal
      members cost $41 vs $18.' (takeaway)
8:00 'Recommendation: 90-day holdout, not full rollout.' (judgment)
10:00 Questions. Every minute answers 'why should we hire you?'
```

modules.title: GitHub Portfolio Engineering
modules.summary: Turn GitHub into a hiring asset: clean repo structures, READMEs that frame problem/approach/results, notebooks that render without errors, pinned repos, requirements files, and commit hygiene that signals professional engineering habits.
objectives: Set up a GitHub profile and repositories engineered for hiring-manager skimming.
Write READMEs, pin environments, and structure repos so analyses reproduce in 30 minutes.
Use GitHub Pages or static exports to publish dashboards and reports as clickable artifacts.
Maintain the portfolio with contribution habits that signal an active practitioner.

notes.title: Profile engineering: the 10-second scan
notes.body:
Hiring managers scan your GitHub profile in seconds: pinned repos (your 3 best projects), a profile README (who you are, what you do, links), and visible recent activity. Unpinned tutorial repos and empty profiles signal 'not serious'.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Profile README template:
# Alex Analyst | Data Analyst
> I turn messy data into decisions. SQL, Python, BI.
- Currently: 7-project analytics portfolio (link)
- Ask me about: experimentation, dashboards that get read
- Contact: email | LinkedIn | portfolio site
Pinned: capstone, SQL deep-dive, A/B test analysis (the 3 strongest).
Unpin: course exercises, forks, half-finished experiments.
The profile answers 'who is this and why interview them' in 10 seconds.
```

notes.title: Repo structure that reproduces
notes.body:
Every project repo: README.md (90-second structure), data/ (or download script — never commit huge files), notebooks/ or src/, requirements.txt or environment.yml, and a reproduce script. Git LFS or download scripts handle large data; .gitignore excludes secrets and outputs.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
project-capstone/
  README.md            # 90-second structure
  data/README.md       # 'Download from <link>; 2.1M rows; caveats...'
  notebooks/01_clean.ipynb  # numbered: clean -> eda -> model -> report
  src/reproduce.py     # one command rebuilds all outputs
  requirements.txt     # pinned versions
  .gitignore           # *.csv, .env, outputs/
Reproduce test: git clone -> pip install -r requirements.txt ->
python src/reproduce.py -> outputs match README. 30 minutes max.
```

notes.title: Git hygiene for analysts
notes.body:
Commit messages say what and why ('Add churn cohort analysis; fixes month-2 gap'). Branch for experiments, merge via PR with a summary. Never commit: credentials, raw PII, or 2GB CSVs. The commit history is a work journal interviewers read.

Worked example (with solution):
```bash
# Analyst git workflow:
git checkout -b experiment/loyalty-holdout   # branch per analysis thread
# ... work ...
git add notebooks/03_loyalty.ipynb
# NEVER: git add data/customers_raw.csv  (PII + huge)
git commit -m "Add loyalty holdout analysis: 22% conversion, $41 CAC"
git push origin experiment/loyalty-holdout
# PR description: question, method, finding, caveats -> merge to main
# History reads as a decision journal, not a dump.
```

notes.title: Publishing: Pages, gists, and static exports
notes.body:
Make work clickable: GitHub Pages hosts project sites and dashboards (exported HTML); gists share single-file analyses; nbviewer renders notebooks without cloning. A link the manager can click beats a repo they must clone.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Publishing ladder (easiest first):
1. Rendered notebook via nbviewer link in the README ('view without cloning').
2. Exported dashboard HTML on GitHub Pages (interactive, zero setup).
3. Project microsite on Pages: question, takeaway, key visual, repo link.
4. Blog writeup (the teaching artifact): 'How I found the month-2 churn leak.'
Each rung removes friction between the hiring manager and your best work.
```

notes.title: Contribution habits that compound
notes.body:
Green squares come from real work: weekly project commits, code reviews on your own PRs, issue tracking for analysis tasks. Quality over gaming: one substantive commit beats ten whitespace tweaks. The habit also keeps skills warm between roles.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sustainable contribution rhythm:
- Weekly: one project commit (analysis progress, documented).
- Per project: issues for each analysis question ('#12: Simpson check by tenure').
- PRs with summaries even when solo (the habit transfers to teams).
- Quarterly: one public artifact (blog post, polished project).
What NOT to do: commit-streak gaming, tutorial repos as 'projects',
forking without contributing. Interviewers can tell.
```

modules.title: Dashboard Portfolio: What Hiring Managers Want
modules.summary: Learn exactly what reviewers scan for in the first 60 seconds of a dashboard, how to run before/after makeovers that prove design judgment, when interactivity adds value versus clutter, and how to publish and write up dashboards that show your thinking.
objectives: Curate dashboard portfolio pieces that prove BI mastery: one decision per dashboard, takeaway titles, honest axes.
Document dashboard build decisions (chart choice, filters, grain) so reviewers see the thinking.
Publish dashboards as clickable artifacts with context (the question, the takeaway, the caveats).
Critique dashboards against the hiring-manager rubric and iterate.

notes.title: What makes a dashboard portfolio-grade
notes.body:
Portfolio dashboards prove: chart choice judgment, filter design, takeaway communication, and honest visualization. Three excellent dashboards beat ten mediocre ones. Each needs: the decision question, the takeaway title, comparison context, and documented caveats.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Portfolio dashboard spec (each of the 3):
Decision: 'Should marketing shift spend from paid search to affiliates?'
Takeaway title: 'Affiliates assist 31% of enterprise deals at 1/3 the CAC.'
Visuals: funnel (assisted vs last-click), CAC comparison bar, trend.
Filters: date range, segment (apply consistently, stated in subtitle).
Caveats: attribution window 90 days; affiliate data 2-day lag.
Grain note: 'One row per touchpoint; deduped to opportunity.'
A reviewer learns your judgment from the spec, not just the pixels.
```

notes.title: The hiring-manager dashboard rubric
notes.body:
Reviewers score: (1) Does the title state a takeaway? (2) Is there comparison context? (3) Are filters consistent and purposeful? (4) Are axes honest? (5) Can I state the decision in 30 seconds? Five yeses = portfolio-grade.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Rubric applied to a candidate dashboard:
1. Title 'Churn concentrates in month 2' -> YES (takeaway, not topic).
2. Bars show current vs prior quarter -> YES (comparison).
3. Region filter affects all 4 sheets -> YES (consistent).
4. Bar y-axes start at zero -> YES (honest).
5. 'Fix onboarding month 2' statable in 30s -> YES (decision-clear).
Score 5/5: publish. 3/5: iterate before publishing.
Use this rubric on YOUR OWN dashboards before anyone else does.
```

notes.title: Documenting build decisions
notes.body:
A build-decisions doc (in the repo) records: why this chart, why these filters, the grain, known caveats, and what you'd do with more time. It turns a pretty dashboard into evidence of judgment — and it's the document you walk through in interviews.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
BUILD DECISIONS (dashboard: affiliate ROI):
- Chart: bars not lines for channel comparison (position > angle).
- Filters: date + segment only (the stakeholder's next questions; every
  additional filter was cut as noise).
- Grain: one row per opportunity-touch; deduped on opportunity_id.
- Caveat: 90-day attribution window; affiliate feed lags 2 days.
- With more time: incrementality test to separate correlation from lift.
The last line ('with more time') shows senior self-awareness.
```

notes.title: Publishing dashboards that get clicked
notes.body:
Export to static HTML or publish to a free tier; embed in the project microsite with the decision question above and the takeaway below. Test on mobile (hiring managers browse on phones). Loading time matters: aggregate before publishing, not in the browser.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Publishing checklist:
- Exported HTML < 5MB (aggregated data, not row-level).
- Decision question as the page H1; takeaway as the subhead.
- Tested on a phone: titles readable, filters tappable.
- Caveats in a visible footnote (not buried).
- Link from the repo README + the portfolio microsite.
A dashboard nobody can open might as well not exist.
```

notes.title: Iterating: the critique cycle
notes.body:
Portfolio dashboards improve through critique cycles: self-review against the rubric, peer review (trade with another analyst), and the 30-second test with a non-analyst. Each cycle fixes one class of issues; three cycles is usually enough.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Critique cycle log:
Cycle 1 (self): titles were topics -> rewrote as takeaways.
Cycle 2 (peer): filters affected 3 of 5 sheets -> made consistent.
Cycle 3 (non-analyst friend): 'What am I supposed to decide?' -> added
  the decision question as H1 and a recommendation callout.
Document the cycles in the repo: the iteration log IS the growth story
interviewers love ('show me how you improved something').
```

notes.title: Capstone scoping: the one-page brief
notes.body:
The capstone brief fits one page: the decision, why it matters (dollars), the data (sources, grain, access), the methods, the risks (what could kill it), and the timeline with milestones. If the brief doesn't fit one page, the scope is wrong.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
CAPSTONE BRIEF: Should Northwind expand its loyalty program?
Why it matters: loyalty members are 18% of customers, 34% of revenue.
Data: orders (2.1M rows, grain: line item), loyalty table, marketing spend.
Methods: cohort retention, CAC comparison, Simpson check by tenure,
  sensitivity analysis on attribution window.
Risks: loyalty table has 12% dup keys (dedup plan); attribution is
  correlational (holdout recommended, not claimed).
Timeline: W1 scope+data, W2 SQL/pandas, W3 stats+viz, W4 report+deck.
Done when: 10-min walkthrough + reproducible repo + stakeholder deck.
```

notes.title: Execution: the full stack in four weeks
notes.body:
Week 1: scope + data audit (profile everything, document caveats). Week 2: SQL + pandas analysis (answer the question three ways, reconcile). Week 3: statistics + visualization (CIs, segments, takeaway-first charts). Week 4: report + deck + walkthrough rehearsal. Each week ends with a reviewable artifact.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Week 2 reconciliation (the senior habit):
  SQL:    loyalty revenue share = 34.2%
  pandas: loyalty revenue share = 34.2%
  Excel spot-check (100-row sample): 34% (rounding)
All three agree -> the number is real. If they disagreed, the DEFINITIONS
differ (filters, NULLs, dups): reconcile before proceeding.
Week 3 Simpson check: loyalty lift holds within tenure bands (not a mix
artifact). Week 4: the deck leads with the recommendation.
The capstone is 4 reconciled weeks, not 4 weeks of hoping.
```

notes.title: The report: structure that persuades
notes.body:
Capstone report structure: executive summary (decision + takeaway + recommendation, one page), question & data (with caveats), methods (just enough to trust), findings (takeaway-first visuals), risks & limits, recommendation, appendix (reproducibility). Write the executive summary LAST.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (one page):
Decision: expand loyalty? Recommendation: 90-day holdout in 3 regions,
  not full rollout.
Takeaway: members retain 2x, but the lift concentrates in tenured users;
  marginal members cost $41 CAC vs $18 for the core.
Evidence: cohort chart, CAC bridge, Simpson-checked segments.
Risk: attribution is correlational; the holdout measures true lift.
Ask: approve the holdout ($120K test budget).
A executive reads this page and decides. Everything else is due diligence.
```

notes.title: The 10-minute walkthrough: rehearsed, not read
notes.body:
The walkthrough is a performance: 10 minutes, no reading slides, every visual introduced by its takeaway. Rehearse with a timer; plant the 3 questions you'll get (data limits, method choice, 'what would you do differently') and answer them before they're asked.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Walkthrough beats (rehearsed):
0:00 The decision + my recommendation (up front).
1:30 The data: 3 tables, grain, the 12% dup-key fix (messiness handled).
3:30 Method in 3 bullets (cohorts, CAC, Simpson check).
5:30 Findings: 2 visuals, takeaways stated before showing.
7:30 Risks: correlational attribution -> holdout recommendation (honesty).
9:00 The ask: approve the $120K test.
9:30 Buffer for questions.
Rehearse 5x with a timer. Record once; watch for filler words and
'so basically' hedging. The walkthrough is the interview.
```

notes.title: Pre-mortem and reproducibility audit
notes.body:
Pre-mortem: 'It's six months later and the capstone failed. Why?' List the failure modes (data went stale, method was wrong, recommendation ignored) and harden against them now. Reproducibility audit: fresh clone, follow README, verify every number.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Pre-mortem (capstone):
- 'The loyalty table refreshed with a new schema; my queries broke.'
  -> Harden: schema-check gate in the reproduce script.
- 'An interviewer found the Simpson problem I missed.'
  -> Harden: segment every finding by the top 2 confounders NOW.
- 'Nobody could reproduce it.'
  -> Harden: the 30-minute stranger test before calling it done.
Reproducibility audit: new machine, clone, pip install, run, diff outputs
vs README. Every mismatch fixed, not explained away.
Done = brief + 4 weeks + report + walkthrough + pre-mortem + audit.
```

notes.body:

notes.title: The loop, stage by stage
notes.body:
Typical senior analyst loop: recruiter screen (background, comp expectations), hiring-manager screen (scope fit), technical rounds (SQL live, stats/probability, take-home or case), behavioral (STAR stories), final (presentation or panel). Each stage filters differently; prepare per stage, not generically.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Stage-by-stage prep:
Recruiter (15-30 min): 2-min pitch, comp range researched, 3 questions.
Hiring manager (45 min): scope stories (stakeholders, decisions influenced).
SQL live (45-60 min): narrate-first; the 6-pattern drill set.
Stats/probability (45 min): Bayes, CIs, A/B design from this course.
Case/take-home (3-5 hrs): capstone walkthrough format.
Behavioral (45 min): 5 STAR stories with numbers.
Final/panel: 10-min capstone walkthrough + Q&A.
One generic prep fails all stages; stage-specific prep passes each.
```

notes.title: The technical question bank
notes.body:
SQL: top-N per group, funnel, streaks, MoM, dedup, anti-join (this course's drills). Stats: Bayes with base rates, CI interpretation, A/B design, Simpson's paradox. Product: metric design, trade-offs, estimation. Behavioral: disagreement, failure, influence, mentoring, ambiguity.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Two-week technical sprint (1 hr/day):
Days 1-3: SQL patterns (2/day, narrated, timed).
Days 4-5: probability (Bayes + counting, with closers).
Days 6-7: A/B design (write 3 experiment plans).
Days 8-9: product sense (metric design for 2 products).
Day 10: estimation (3 Fermi problems, structured).
Days 11-12: behavioral stories (write + rehearse 5 STARs).
Days 13-14: full mock loop (below).
Sprint output: a personal 'miss log' driving the next sprint.
```

notes.title: Mock loops: realistic conditions
notes.body:
Mocks must simulate pressure: timed, camera on, stranger interviewer (peer swap), no pausing. Record; review against a rubric (correctness, narration, edge cases, communication). One mock per week during active search; the miss log becomes the drill list.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Mock rubric (score 1-5 each):
- Correctness: right answer, verified.
- Narration: restated, grain stated, thinking aloud.
- Edge cases: NULLs, dups, ties, timezones named.
- Communication: takeaway-first, no rambling.
- Poise: handled the follow-up without flustering.
After: top 2 misses -> 20-min drills each, re-mock in 3 days.
The loop that improves: mock -> rubric -> drills -> re-mock.
Mocks without rubrics are just anxiety practice.
```

notes.title: Take-homes and case presentations
notes.body:
Take-homes test judgment under realistic conditions: scope the question, document assumptions, show method, state takeaways, note limits. Timebox ruthlessly (the stated hours, not 3x). The presentation: 10-minute walkthrough + Q&A; they probe choices, not polish.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Take-home rules:
1. Read twice; restate the decision in your own words (in the doc).
2. Assumptions section FIRST (they grade your judgment here).
3. Method: 3 bullets, not a textbook.
4. Takeaway-first visuals; caveats visible.
5. 'With more time' section (scope awareness).
6. Ship at the timebox: completeness within limits beats perfection late.
Presentation: the capstone walkthrough format. Q&A prep: for every
choice, know the alternative you rejected and why.
```

notes.title: Offers and negotiation
notes.body:
Evaluate offers on: total comp (base + bonus + equity, annualized), scope (team, decisions, data access), manager (your growth lever), and trajectory (what the next role looks like). Negotiate with competing timelines honestly; never fabricate competing offers.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Offer evaluation sheet:
- Base / bonus target / equity (4-yr, vesting) -> annualized total.
- Scope: team size, stakeholder level, decision rights.
- Manager: 1:1 cadence? growth track record?
- Trajectory: what does promotion look like in 18 months?
- Logistics: remote/hybrid, hours expectations.
Negotiation script: 'I'm excited about the scope. Based on [market data
+ competing timeline], I was targeting [range]. Is there flexibility?'
One round, honest, data-backed. Then decide and commit fully.
```

handsOnLab.brief: Build your personalized 90-day plan: calendar, cert schedule, portfolio milestones, pipeline targets, and accountability structure.
steps: Audit your current state (skills, portfolio, certs) honestly.

mockTask.explain: Read the funnel stage by stage: fix the breaking stage, not the whole machine.

notes.title: The 90-day architecture
notes.body:
90 days, three phases: Days 1-30 (skill sprints + portfolio projects 1-3 + cert #1 study), Days 31-60 (portfolio 4-6 + cert #1 exam + applications begin), Days 61-90 (capstone + cert #2 + full application pipeline + interviews). Certifications and portfolio interleave; applications start when proof exists, not before.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Week-by-week (10 hrs/day full-time search):
W1-2:  SQL sprint + portfolio P1 (SQL deep-dive) + Google cert courses 1-2
W3-4:  pandas sprint + P2 + cert courses 3-4
W5-6:  stats/A-B sprint + P3 + cert courses 5-6; EXAM Google cert
W7-8:  BI sprint + P4 (dashboard) + PL-300 study begins; 5 apps/week start
W9-10: Excel + P5; PL-300 exam; 10 apps/week
W11:   Domain project P6; interview prep sprint begins
W12:   Capstone + 15 apps/week + mock loops
Adjust hours to your reality; the SEQUENCE is what matters.
```

notes.title: Certification ROI: which, when, when to stop
notes.body:
Certifications have diminishing returns: the first proves baseline, the second adds a specialty, the third is procrastination. ROI order for analysts: one broad (Google DA), one tool-depth (PL-300 or Tableau), then STOP and let the portfolio + interviews carry. Never certify instead of applying.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Cert decision matrix:
Google Data Analytics: broad baseline, portfolio-friendly -> FIRST.
PL-300: Power BI depth for BI-heavy roles -> SECOND (if targeting BI roles).
Tableau Certified: viz depth -> SECOND (if targeting Tableau shops).
Data+: vendor-neutral breadth -> alternative first cert.
STOP rule: after 2 certs, every additional study hour goes to applications
and interview prep. The third cert's marginal interview value ~= 0.
Exam-day: sleep > cramming; scenario questions reward rested judgment.
```

notes.title: The application pipeline
notes.body:
Treat applications as a pipeline: target list (20-30 companies, researched), tailored resume per role (mirror the posting's language), portfolio link in every application, tracking spreadsheet (company, role, date, stage, follow-up), and follow-up cadence (7 days, then 21).

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Pipeline metrics (weekly review):
- Applications sent: 10-15/week (quality > spray).
- Response rate: target 15-25% (below 10%: fix resume/portfolio).
- Screen -> technical: target 50% (below: drill the weak stage).
- Technical -> final: target 30%.
- Offer rate per final: 25-35%.
Funnel math: 12 apps/week x 12 weeks = 144 apps -> ~25 screens ->
~12 technicals -> ~4 finals -> ~1-2 offers. Work the funnel, not luck.
Tailoring: 20 min per application (mirror posting language, reorder bullets).
```

notes.title: Interview prep integration
notes.body:
Prep integrates with the pipeline: SQL drills daily (15 min), one mock per week once screens start, STAR stories written before the first interview, capstone walkthrough rehearsed before finals. Prep without pipeline is rehearsal without a stage; pipeline without prep wastes opportunities.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Weekly rhythm (active search):
Mon-Fri: 15-min SQL drill (morning) + applications (2-3/day).
Wed: 1-hr stats/probability review (rotate topics).
Sat: mock loop (alternating: SQL live / case / behavioral).
Sun: miss-log review + drill plan for the week.
The 15-min daily drill compounds: 90 days x 15 min = 22 hours of SQL
fluency. Consistency beats cramming; the miss log aims the work.
```

notes.title: Momentum: routines and burnout guards
notes.body:
A 90-day search is a marathon: fixed work hours, one full day off weekly, exercise, and a weekly review (metrics + feelings). Burnout signals: dreading applications, doomscrolling instead of drills, skipping mocks. The fix is structural (rest, smaller batches), not motivational.

Worked example (with solution):
```text
Sustainable search rules:
- Work 9-5 on the search; evenings are yours (no 'one more application').
- One full day off per week (recovery is productive).
- Weekly review: pipeline metrics + energy check (1-5).
- Accountability: one partner for weekly check-ins (or this course's plan).
- Rejection protocol: log it, extract one lesson, next application within 24h.
Rejections are funnel data, not verdicts: 144 apps -> 1-2 offers means
~142 rejections are the PLAN working, not failing.
```

cards.back: An in-process, columnar, vectorized analytical SQL engine: one library install, no server, queries CSV/Parquet/dataframes directly.
SQLite is row-store OLTP (transactions); DuckDB is column-store OLAP (aggregations). Both embedded, different workloads.

cards.front: Why columnar storage wins for analytics
cards.back: Columns stored contiguously; aggregations scan only the columns they need, in vectorized batches, skipping irrelevant data.

cards.front: Query a pandas dataframe with SQL
cards.back: con.execute('SELECT ... FROM my_df') — DuckDB sees Python-scope dataframes as tables; return with .df(), .pl(), or .arrow().
Filters on window-function results without a wrapping subquery: e.g. QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cat ORDER BY rev DESC) <= 3.
Reshapes long category rows into wide columns (one per region/channel) in SQL, producing dashboard-shaped output.
duckdb.connect() is in-memory (vanishes on exit); duckdb.connect('file.duckdb') persists tables across sessions.
COPY (SELECT ...) TO 'out.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET) — exports curated query results for dbt, BI extracts, or cloud upload.

cards.front: Define: Lock in the essentials of DuckDB for Analytics before the drills.
cards.back: **Install DuckDB and run analytical SQL against CSV and Parquet files with no server setup** — if you cannot explain this in two sentences without looking, re-read the notes above before attempting the drills.

cards.front: Why is DuckDB typically faster than a row-store database for a SUM over 10M rows?
cards.back: It stores each column contiguously and processes data in vectorized batches, scanning only needed columns — Columnar layout + vectorized execution is the core performance story: minimal I/O, batch CPU processing. (Module 41)

cards.front: You have a pandas dataframe `df` and want the average of column `x` by `g` using DuckDB, returned as pandas. Which is correct?
cards.back: con.execute('SELECT g, AVG(x) AS a FROM df GROUP BY g').df() — Dataframes in scope are queryable as tables; .df() returns a pandas frame. (Module 41)

cards.front: What does QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) <= 3 do?
cards.back: Keeps the top 3 rows by revenue without needing a subquery around the window function — QUALIFY filters on window results directly — the idiom for top-N-per-group in one pass. (Module 41)

choices: DuckDB auto-registers CSV readers as table functions
CSV files are always loaded into memory first
DuckDB converts CSV to Parquet on disk first
The csv extension must be manually INSTALLed before any read
items.explain: read_csv is a built-in table function — DuckDB infers schema and reads the file lazily without a separate load step.
items.q: You run: SELECT * FROM read_csv('sales_2024.csv'); In DuckDB this works because:

choices: SELECT region, STDDEV_SAMP(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY region;
SELECT region, VARIANCE(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY 1;
SELECT DISTINCT region, STDEV(revenue) OVER () FROM sales;
items.explain: STDDEV_SAMP (alias STDDEV) with GROUP BY computes per-region sample standard deviation. DuckDB supports both STDDEV_SAMP and STDDEV_POP.
items.q: Which query correctly computes the sample standard deviation of revenue per region using a single pass?

choices: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM read_parquet('f.parquet') WHERE year=2024;
COPY f.parquet to CSV then filter;
Load the whole file into pandas first;

notes.title: Why DuckDB exists: the embedded analytics gap
notes.body:
- Before DuckDB, the analyst's choices were: a heavyweight server database (Postgres, SQL Server) for real SQL, or an in-memory dataframe for speed — nothing fast, SQL-first, and zero-infrastructure in between.
- DuckDB fills that gap: a single library (pip install duckdb) that runs the full analytical SQL dialect inside your Python process, on files sitting on disk.
- It is columnar (stores each column contiguously) and vectorized (processes data in batches, not row by row), which is why aggregations over millions of rows feel instant while the same query crawls on a row-store.
- Mental model: SQLite is to row-store OLTP what DuckDB is to column-store OLAP. SQLite for transactions, DuckDB for analytics.
- Senior-bar framing: know when embedded is enough (exploration, interview take-homes, CI data tests) and when you graduate to a warehouse (concurrent writers, governed access, TB-scale storage).

```python
# One install, zero servers, query a CSV like a table
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect()  # in-memory; pass a filename for a persistent file DB
result = con.execute("""
  SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM read_csv('orders.csv', header=true)
  GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC
""").df()
print(result)
```

notes.title: Zero-copy handoff with pandas and Polars
notes.body:
- The killer feature for analysts: DuckDB can query your existing dataframes directly — `FROM my_df` — and hand results back as a dataframe with no serialization cost in the common paths.
- Going SQL-first keeps logic in one language (SQL) and lets the engine optimize; going dataframe-first keeps you in Python when the logic is procedural. DuckDB lets you mix per-query.
- Register a dataframe once (`con.register('df', pandas_df)`) or reference it by variable name inline.
- Read results as pandas with `.df()`, as Polars with `.pl()`, as Arrow with `.arrow()` — pick the frame your downstream code expects.

```python
import duckdb, pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({
  'order_id': [1, 2, 3, 4],
  'region': ['East', 'West', 'East', 'West'],
  'amount': [120.0, 85.5, 200.0, 40.0]
})
con = duckdb.connect()
# Query the pandas dataframe with SQL, get a pandas dataframe back
avg_by_region = con.execute(
  "SELECT region, AVG(amount) AS avg_order FROM orders GROUP BY region"
).df()
# Same query, Polars output
avg_pl = con.execute(
  "SELECT region, AVG(amount) AS avg_order FROM orders GROUP BY region"
).pl()
```

notes.title: Window functions and multi-step questions in one query
notes.body:
- DuckDB ships a full modern SQL dialect: window functions, CTEs, QUALIFY (filter on window results without a subquery), and PIVOT.
- QUALIFY is the idiom interviewers love: rank-then-filter in a single pass, e.g. 'top 3 products per category by revenue'.
- PIVOT turns long-format category rows into wide-format columns for dashboard-shaped output — do it in SQL so the BI tool receives a tidy table.
- Worked example pattern: CTE builds monthly revenue, window function adds running total and month-over-month growth, QUALIFY keeps the top months.

```sql
-- Running totals + MoM growth + top-3 months, one query
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM read_csv('orders.csv', header=true)
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_revenue,
       revenue / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) - 1 AS mom_growth
FROM monthly
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) <= 3
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

```sql
-- PIVOT: one column per region for a dashboard feed
PIVOT read_csv('orders.csv', header=true)
ON region USING SUM(amount) GROUP BY date_trunc('month', order_date);
```

notes.title: Repeatable local workflow: persist, cache, export
notes.body:
- Default `duckdb.connect()` is in-memory: results vanish when the process ends. Pass a filename (`duckdb.connect('analytics.duckdb')`) and tables persist between sessions.
- Pattern: ingest raw files once into a persistent `.duckdb` file, then run all exploration against the stored tables — faster than re-parsing CSVs every run and reproducible.
- `COPY (SELECT ...) TO 'out.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET)` writes query results to Parquet for downstream tools (dbt, Tableau extracts, S3 uploads).
- ATTACH lets one query read from another database file — useful for joining a staging DB with a curated DB without copying data.
- Discipline: the same data-validation habits apply — check row counts and nulls after ingest, because a local file DB has no warehouse governance watching it for you.

```python
import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect('analytics.duckdb')
# Ingest once, query many times
con.execute("CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE orders AS FROM read_csv('orders.csv', header=true)")
print(con.execute('SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(amount) FROM orders').fetchall())  # null check
# Export a curated table for the BI layer
con.execute("COPY (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount > 0) TO 'orders_clean.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET)")
```

**Analyst's notebook: how this topic shows up in real data work.**

*DuckDB for Analytics* earns its keep when a stakeholder asks a question the dashboard can't answer. The professional pattern is always the same: clarify the business question first, check the data's fitness second, do the analysis third — never the reverse.

- **The question behind the question.** 'Can you pull the numbers?' usually means 'help me decide X'. Get the decision on the table before touching data.
- **Garbage in, gospel out.** No amount of modeling fixes mislabeled, duplicated, or stale source data. Profile the data before analyzing it.

- **Show your work.** Assumptions, filters, and exclusions belong in the deliverable, not in your head. Reproducibility is what separates analysis from opinion.
- **Answer, then caveat.** Lead with the finding and its confidence; put methodology and limitations after, not before.

notes.title: Two engines, two philosophies
notes.body:
- pandas (2008): eager — every operation executes immediately and materializes a result; single-threaded; built on NumPy; the biggest API surface and ecosystem in data Python.
- Polars (2020): lazy-first — `.lazy()` builds a query plan that the optimizer rewrites before executing; multithreaded in Rust; columnar Arrow-based memory.
- The practical consequence: a 5-step pandas chain runs 5 passes over the data; Polars' optimizer can fuse them, skip unneeded columns, and push filters down to the file scan.
- Neither is 'the winner'. pandas wins on ecosystem (every library accepts a DataFrame) and hiring-manager familiarity; Polars wins on raw speed, memory, and large-file handling.

```python
import pandas as pd
# pandas: eager, each step runs now
pdf = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
out = (pdf[pdf['amount'] > 100]
           .groupby('region')['amount'].sum()
           .reset_index())

import polars as pl
# Polars: lazy plan, optimized, then executed
out2 = (pl.scan_csv('orders.csv')
          .filter(pl.col('amount') > 100)
          .group_by('region')
          .agg(pl.col('amount').sum())
          .collect())
```

notes.title: Syntax mapping: read one, write the other
notes.body:
- The 80% mapping analysts need: `df[df.x > 1]` → `df.filter(pl.col('x') > 1)`; `.groupby().agg()` → `.group_by().agg()`; `.merge()` → `.join()`; `df['new'] = ...` → `.with_columns(...)`.
- Polars expressions (`pl.col('x').str.to_uppercase().alias('X')`) compose inside a single `with_columns` — one pass, many new columns; pandas assignment is one pass per column.
- Nulls: pandas uses NaN/None/NaT inconsistently; Polars has a strict null type — `fill_null`, `drop_nulls`, and `is_null()` behave uniformly, which reduces silent bugs.
- Strings and dates have dedicated namespaces (`.str`, `.dt`) in both, but Polars' are vectorized in Rust with no Python-loop fallback temptation.

```python
import polars as pl
# One with_columns, many derived columns, single pass
clean = (pl.read_csv('orders.csv')
  .with_columns([
    pl.col('region').str.to_uppercase().alias('region'),
    pl.col('order_date').str.to_date('%Y-%m-%d').alias('order_date'),
    pl.col('amount').fill_null(0).alias('amount'),
  ])
  .filter(pl.col('amount') >= 0))

# Join: explicit keys, explicit how — same idea as pandas merge
joined = clean.join(customers, on='customer_id', how='left')
```

notes.title: Lazy evaluation and what the optimizer does for you
notes.body:
- Lazy = describe the computation, execute later. `scan_csv` + transforms + `.collect()` lets Polars see the whole plan before touching data.
- Predicate pushdown: a `.filter()` written after the scan is pushed INTO the file read, so rows are skipped during parsing instead of loaded then dropped.
- Projection pushdown: only columns used downstream are read from disk — a 50-column CSV with a 3-column query reads 3 columns.
- `.explain()` prints the optimized plan — the single best debugging tool when a query is slow: read the plan before guessing.
- Interview framing: 'lazy evaluation lets the engine optimize the whole query graph, like a SQL planner, instead of executing each step blindly.'

```python
import polars as pl
q = (pl.scan_csv('orders.csv')
       .filter(pl.col('amount') > 100)   # pushed into the scan
       .select(['region', 'amount']))     # only 2 columns read
print(q.explain())  # read the optimized plan
result = q.collect()  # nothing ran until this line
```

notes.title: Decision rules: which frame, when
notes.body:
- Choose pandas when: the downstream library demands it (statsmodels, many sklearn paths), the team standard is pandas, or the data fits comfortably in memory and speed is fine.
- Choose Polars when: files are large relative to RAM, the pipeline is slow and profiling blames pandas, you want multithreading for free, or you are writing new ETL.
- Never choose on hype: benchmark YOUR query on YOUR data. A 10k-row groupby will not care which engine you use; a 100M-row one will.
- Migration tactic: new modules in Polars, old code untouched; convert at the boundary (`.to_pandas()` / `pl.from_pandas()`) rather than big-bang rewrites.
- The meta-skill interviewers test: can you reason about the tradeoff (ecosystem vs performance vs team norms) instead of reciting a preference?

```python
import time, polars as pl, pandas as pd
# Benchmark YOUR workload, not a blog's
t0 = time.perf_counter()
(pd.read_csv('orders.csv').groupby('region')['amount'].sum())
pandas_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
(pl.scan_csv('orders.csv').group_by('region').agg(pl.col('amount').sum()).collect())
polars_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f'pandas {pandas_s:.2f}s  polars {polars_s:.2f}s')
```

notes.title: The problem Iceberg solves: files are not tables
notes.body:
- A data lake full of Parquet files is cheap storage, but files alone give you no transactions (two writers can corrupt each other), no consistent snapshot reads, and painful schema changes.
- A table format is a metadata layer on top of the files: it tracks which files belong to the table, what the schema is, and the history of changes — so readers always see a consistent view.
- Iceberg's design: a metadata file points to a snapshot; the snapshot points to manifest files; manifests list the actual data files. Every write creates a NEW snapshot — old snapshots stay, which is what makes time travel possible.
- ACID in plain terms: a write either fully lands as a new snapshot or it doesn't — readers never see a half-written table.

```sql
-- DuckDB can read an Iceberg table's metadata: which snapshots exist?
SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, summary
FROM iceberg_snapshots('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
```

notes.title: Time travel: reproducible analysis without backups
notes.body:
- Because every write is a new immutable snapshot, you can query the table exactly as it looked at any past snapshot or timestamp.
- Analyst use cases: 're-run last quarter's report on the data as it was then' (reproducibility), 'what did this row look like before the backfill?' (debugging), incident forensics.
- Two flavors: by snapshot id (exact) or by timestamp (as-of — resolves to the latest snapshot before that time).
- Discipline: time travel shows you old DATA, not old LOGIC — re-running an old query file against an old snapshot is the full reproducibility story; pair both in version control.

```sql
-- What did the table look like before today's backfill?
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount) AS revenue_then
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg',
                  version => '2026-10-01 00:00:00');

-- Compare then vs now in one query
WITH then_t AS (
  SELECT SUM(amount) AS rev FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg', version => '2026-10-01 00:00:00')
),
now_t AS (
  SELECT SUM(amount) AS rev FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg')
)
SELECT then_t.rev AS revenue_oct1, now_t.rev AS revenue_now,
       now_t.rev - then_t.rev AS delta_from_backfill
FROM then_t, now_t;
```

notes.title: Hidden partitioning: stop thinking about directories
notes.body:
- Traditional Hive-style partitioning bakes the partition into the directory path (year=2026/month=10/...) — queries must know the layout, and changing the partition scheme means rewriting all the data.
- Iceberg's hidden partitioning: you declare a partition transform (e.g. day(order_date), bucket(customer_id, 16)) in the table metadata; the engine maps each row to its partition automatically.
- The analyst benefit: you write `WHERE order_date >= '2026-10-01'` on the plain column — no partition-column gymnastics — and the engine prunes files that can't match.
- Partition evolution: change the partition scheme later (month -> day) and old files keep working — old and new layouts coexist, queries stay the same.

```sql
-- Create an Iceberg table with hidden partitioning via DuckDB
CREATE TABLE orders_iceberg AS
FROM read_csv('orders.csv', header=true);
-- (Conceptually: PARTITIONED BY days(order_date), bucket(customer_id, 16))
-- The analyst query stays clean — pruning happens under the hood:
SELECT region, SUM(amount)
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg')
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-10-01'   -- engine skips non-matching files
GROUP BY region;
```

notes.title: Schema evolution without the rewrite
notes.body:
- In plain Parquet lakes, adding a column means rewriting files or living with inconsistent schemas across partitions.
- Iceberg tracks columns by ID, not position: add a column, rename one, or widen a type (int -> bigint), and old files are read with the new schema — missing values come back as null.
- What you still can't do casually: narrowing types or dropping columns that downstream jobs depend on — evolution is safe, not magic.
- Analyst habit: when a source adds a field mid-quarter, evolve the Iceberg schema forward and document the change date; historical queries keep working because old snapshots keep the old schema view.

```sql
-- Inspect current schema, then evolve it (conceptual DDL)
SELECT field_name, field_type
FROM iceberg_schema('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
-- ALTER TABLE orders_iceberg ADD COLUMN promo_code VARCHAR;
-- Old files: promo_code reads back as NULL. New files: populated.
-- Query across the evolution boundary safely:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_before,
       COUNT(promo_code) AS rows_with_promo
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
```

**Analyst's notebook: how this topic shows up in real data work.**

*Apache Iceberg Concepts: Table Format, Time Travel, Partitioning* earns its keep when a stakeholder asks a question the dashboard can't answer. The professional pattern is always the same: clarify the business question first, check the data's fitness second, do the analysis third — never the reverse.

- **The question behind the question.** 'Can you pull the numbers?' usually means 'help me decide X'. Get the decision on the table before touching data.
- **Garbage in, gospel out.** No amount of modeling fixes mislabeled, duplicated, or stale source data. Profile the data before analyzing it.
- **One chart, one message.** If a visualization needs a paragraph to explain, redesign it. The takeaway should survive a three-second glance.
- **Show your work.** Assumptions, filters, and exclusions belong in the deliverable, not in your head. Reproducibility is what separates analysis from opinion.
- **Answer, then caveat.** Lead with the finding and its confidence; put methodology and limitations after, not before.

notes.title: The dbt mental model: SQL with software discipline
notes.body:
- Without dbt: analysts keep 40 SQL files named final_v2_ACTUAL.sql, nobody knows the run order, and 'it worked on my laptop' is the deployment story.
- With dbt: each model is one SELECT statement in a .sql file; dbt compiles them in dependency order, materializes them as tables/views, and versions everything in git.
- `ref('stg_orders')` = 'build the model named stg_orders first, then use it' — dbt draws the DAG from your ref() calls, so run order is derived, never hand-scheduled.
- `source('raw', 'orders')` = 'read the raw table orders from the raw schema' — sources are declared once in YAML, so every model references raw data the same way.

```sql
-- models/marts/orders_daily.sql: a model is just a SELECT
WITH cleaned AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
    amount
  FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}   -- dbt resolves the dependency
  WHERE amount >= 0
)
SELECT
  order_date,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM cleaned
GROUP BY order_date
```

notes.title: Project layout: staging, intermediate, marts
notes.body:
- Convention (not law): staging (stg_) = 1:1 with sources, light cleaning, renamed columns; intermediate (int_) = reusable business logic; marts = wide, analytics-ready tables per domain.
- Materializations: view (default, always fresh, slower), table (persisted, rebuilt each run), incremental (append/update new rows — for large tables).
- Choose per model: small dimensions -> table; huge event logs -> incremental; exploratory -> view.
- Every model gets a YAML entry: description + column descriptions — this is what becomes documentation, and 'undocumented model' is a code-review fail.

```yaml
# models/marts/_marts.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: orders_daily
    description: "One row per day: order counts and revenue, cleaned. Grain: order_date."
    columns:
      - name: order_date
        description: "Calendar date of the order. Primary grain of this mart."
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: revenue
        description: "Sum of order amounts for the day, refunds excluded."
```

```bash
# Run it locally against DuckDB
 dbt build --profiles-dir .   # builds models, runs tests, in DAG order
```

notes.title: Tests: the data contract you run every time
notes.body:
- Generic tests (built in): unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships (foreign-key check). Declared in YAML, run on every build.
- Singular tests: custom SQL files in tests/ that must return ZERO rows — any row returned is a failure. This is where business rules live ('no negative revenue', 'no future order dates').
- Test severity: error (default, blocks) vs warn (logs, continues) — warn for new rules you're calibrating, error once trusted.
- Senior habit: a model without tests is a draft. Tests are how you prove the pipeline, not just the query, is correct.

```yaml
# generic tests live in the model's YAML
columns:
  - name: order_id
    tests: [unique, not_null]
  - name: customer_id
    tests:
      - relationships:
          to: ref('dim_customers')
          field: customer_id
```

```sql
-- tests/no_future_orders.sql: singular test, must return 0 rows
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
WHERE order_date > CURRENT_DATE
```

notes.title: Docs and lineage: dbt docs generate
notes.body:
- `dbt docs generate` + `dbt docs serve` builds a local website: every model, its SQL, its column descriptions, its tests and their status, and the full lineage DAG.
- Lineage answers the stakeholder question 'where does this dashboard number come from?' — click the mart, walk the graph back to raw sources.
- Exposures (declared in YAML) link dashboards to the models that feed them, so a model change shows which dashboards are affected.
- Workflow discipline: dbt build (models+tests) -> dbt docs generate -> review lineage before merging. Docs are a build artifact, not a wiki page you write later.

```yaml
# models/exposures.yml — tie the dashboard to its models
version: 2
exposures:
  - name: executive_revenue_dashboard
    type: dashboard
    owner: {name: analytics-team}
    depends_on:
      - ref('orders_daily')
      - ref('dim_customers')
```

```bash
dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve --port 8080
# open localhost:8080 -> lineage graph, column docs, test results
```

notes.title: Streamlit: the script that became an app
notes.body:
- Streamlit turns a Python script into a web app: every widget interaction reruns the script top to bottom, and Streamlit diffs the output into the page.
- The rerun model is simple but has a cost: expensive data loads rerun too — unless cached. `@st.cache_data` memoizes function results (dataframes, query results); `@st.cache_resource` holds singletons (DB connections, models).
- Layout primitives: `st.sidebar` for controls, `st.columns` for side-by-side KPIs, `st.tabs` for views, `st.expander` for details. Keep controls in the sidebar so the main canvas stays a clean story.
- Worked pattern: load once (cached), filter with widgets, show KPIs + chart + raw table with download button.

```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

@st.cache_data
def load_orders():
    return pd.read_csv('orders_clean.parquet')

st.title('Orders overview')
df = load_orders()
regions = st.sidebar.multiselect('Region', df['region'].unique(), default=list(df['region'].unique()))
min_amt = st.sidebar.slider('Min amount', 0, 1000, 0)
view = df[(df['region'].isin(regions)) & (df['amount'] >= min_amt)]

c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
c1.metric('Orders', f"{len(view):,}")
c2.metric('Revenue', f"${view['amount'].sum():,.0f}")
c3.metric('Avg order', f"${view['amount'].mean():,.2f}")
st.bar_chart(view.groupby('region')['amount'].sum())
st.download_button('Download filtered CSV', view.to_csv(index=False), 'orders.csv')
```

notes.title: Marimo: reactive notebooks without the hidden-state trap
App structure that survives v1
notes.body:
- The failure mode: one 600-line app.py with SQL strings, business logic, and layout interleaved — unmaintainable by week three.
- Structure: `data.py` (loading/caching, the ONLY place that touches files or DBs), `metrics.py` (KPI computations as pure functions), `app.py` (widgets + layout only).
- Pure functions for metrics = testable without Streamlit; the data layer = swappable (CSV today, warehouse tomorrow) without touching layout.
- Validate inputs at the boundary: empty filter results should show an explicit empty state ('No orders match these filters'), never a blank page or a crash.

```python
# metrics.py — pure functions, no Streamlit imports
def kpis(df):
    return {
        'orders': len(df),
        'revenue': float(df['amount'].sum()),
        'avg_order': float(df['amount'].mean()) if len(df) else 0.0,
    }

# app.py
from metrics import kpis
k = kpis(view)
if not len(view):
    st.warning('No orders match these filters — widen the selection.')
else:
    c1.metric('Orders', f"{k['orders']:,}")
```

notes.title: Shipping and secrets: the honest deployment checklist
notes.body:
- Never hardcode credentials: use environment variables or the platform's secrets manager (`st.secrets`), and keep a `.env.example` (keys, no values) in the repo.
- Pin dependencies (requirements.txt with versions) — an unpinned deploy that breaks on a library update is the classic demo-day failure.
- Add a one-paragraph README: what the app answers, the data source and refresh cadence, who owns it. An app without an owner rots.
- Access honesty: if the data is sensitive, the app needs authentication — a public link to internal revenue data is a security incident, not a deliverable.

```python
# secrets done right: values live in the platform, never in git
import streamlit as st
DB_URL = st.secrets['DB_URL']  # set in the deployment platform's secrets UI
# .env.example (committed):
# DB_URL=postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db   <- placeholder only
```

```bash
# deploy checklist
pip freeze > requirements.txt   # pin everything
# README: question answered, data source + refresh, owner, secrets needed
```

```text
Interview framing that is honest:

centers on OneLake as the single storage namespace, lakehouses that layer
```

notes.title: OneLake: one logical lake
notes.body:
- The problem OneLake addresses: every team provisions its own storage accounts, data gets copied between them, and nobody knows which copy is current — 'data sprawl'.
- The concept: a single logical data lake namespace for the organization. Physically it may span storage, but logically there is one place data lives and one copy to govern.
- Shortcuts (the key idea): virtual references that let a lakehouse or warehouse see data stored elsewhere WITHOUT copying it — one physical copy, many logical views.
- Analyst translation: shortcuts are the managed-service version of 'don't copy the CSV five times; point at it.' The governance win is eliminating divergent copies.

```text
Sprawl (before):  team-a copies orders.csv to their storage,
                   team-b copies it to theirs, team-c exports
                   from the warehouse -> 3 copies, 3 truths.
OneLake (concept): one namespace; teams create shortcuts
                   (pointers, not copies) to the single dataset.
Analyst habit: always ask 'is this a copy or a reference?'
before building on a dataset.
```

notes.title: Lakehouse: warehouse structure on lake economics
notes.body:
- Lakehouse = the architectural pattern (not one product): store data as open files in cheap object storage, then layer warehouse capabilities — transactions, schema enforcement, time travel — via an open table format.
- You already know this pattern from Module 43: Iceberg/Delta-style table formats ARE the lakehouse's transaction layer. Fabric's lakehouse uses Delta Lake as its format.
- Medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold): bronze = raw ingested, silver = cleaned/conformed, gold = business-ready marts. This maps directly onto dbt's staging/intermediate/marts from Module 44.
- Interview move: when asked about Fabric lakehouses, answer in medallion + table-format terms — the concepts are vendor-neutral even when the question isn't.

```text
bronze (raw)      -> land source files as-is, immutable
silver (cleaned)  -> typed, deduplicated, conformed  [= dbt staging/intermediate]
gold (business)   -> aggregated, domain marts        [= dbt marts]
Table format underneath (Delta/Iceberg-style) gives
transactions + time travel at every layer.
```

notes.title: Direct Lake vs import vs DirectQuery
notes.body:
- Import mode (classic BI): data is copied into the BI engine's in-memory store. Fast queries, but copies go stale and large models hit size limits.
- DirectQuery: every visual sends SQL to the source live. Always fresh, but visuals are only as fast as the source, and heavy dashboards can hammer it.
- Direct Lake (the concept): the BI engine queries the lake's table-format files directly — no import copy, no per-visual SQL round trips — because the files are already in an optimized columnar format the engine reads natively.
- Tradeoff in one line: import = speed at the cost of freshness and duplication; DirectQuery = freshness at the cost of speed; Direct Lake tries to get both by making the lake itself the fast store.
- Analyst relevance: when a stakeholder asks 'why is the dashboard stale?', the answer is always about which of these three modes feeds it.

```text
Decision guide (concepts, any platform):
  Need sub-second visuals on <1GB, refresh daily? -> import-style copy is fine.
  Need real-time on a fast source?                     -> live query (DirectQuery-style).
  Need fresh + fast on lake-scale data?                -> Direct Lake-style: query
                                                        optimized lake files directly.
Always document which mode each dashboard uses.
```

notes.title: The pair-programmer contract: AI drafts, you verify
notes.body:
- The productive framing: AI is a fast junior analyst who never sleeps and sometimes lies with perfect grammar. You are the senior who reviews every line.
- Good uses: boilerplate SQL scaffolding, translating logic between dialects, explaining cryptic error messages, generating test cases, drafting narrative around numbers YOU computed.
- The contract: nothing AI generates reaches a stakeholder, a pipeline, or a decision without passing your validation ladder.
- Prompting discipline: give the AI the schema (table/column names), the grain, and the business rule — vague prompts get plausible generic SQL that silently answers the wrong question.

```text
Weak prompt:  "write SQL for monthly revenue"
Strong prompt: "Tables: orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date DATE, amount NUMERIC,
               region VARCHAR). Grain: one row per month. Business rule: exclude
               negative amounts (refunds live in refunds table, ignore them).
               Return month, order_count, revenue. Postgres dialect."

The strong prompt constrains the hallucination surface: real columns,
real rules, real dialect.
```

notes.title: Hallucination patterns analysts must recognize
notes.body:
- Fabricated functions: `SELECT MEDIAN_BY_REGION(...)` — sounds real, doesn't exist. Always check functions against actual docs or by running.
- Plausible-wrong logic: the SQL runs but answers a different question (e.g. averages of averages, or joining on the wrong key that happens to match). Running it is not validating it.
- Invented citations: fake article titles, fake doc URLs, fake 'studies show 73%...' statistics. If a claim matters, find the primary source yourself.
- Sycophancy: the AI agrees with your wrong premise instead of correcting it ('Yes, your join is correct!' when it isn't). Ask it to challenge your logic, not confirm it.
- Defense: the validation ladder below catches all four — no output skips it.

```sql
-- AI gave you this. It RUNS. Is it right?
SELECT region, AVG(daily_rev) AS avg_monthly_revenue
FROM (SELECT region, order_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_rev
      FROM orders GROUP BY region, order_date) d
GROUP BY region;
-- WRONG: average of daily revenues != monthly revenue (days per month vary).
-- Correct: SUM(amount) grouped by month. The AI's version is plausible,
-- executable, and wrong. Only reasoning catches it — running doesn't.
```

notes.title: The validation ladder: run it, count it, spot-check it, explain it
notes.body:
- Rung 1 — Run it: does it execute without error? (Necessary, not sufficient.)
- Rung 2 — Row-count it: do the row counts and totals reconcile with a known baseline? (The orders table has 12,400 rows; your query returns 12,400 or you know why not.)
- Rung 3 — Spot-check it: hand-verify 3-5 rows against source data. Pick edge cases (nulls, boundaries), not just the happy path.
- Rung 4 — Explain it back: can you explain what each clause does and why the grain is correct? If you can't explain it, you can't defend it to a stakeholder.
- Document the assist: in code review or handoff notes, mark AI-generated sections ('drafted with AI assistance, validated per ladder') — transparency is professionalism.

```text
Validation ladder checklist (paste into PR descriptions):
[ ] Rung 1: executes cleanly
[ ] Rung 2: row counts + control totals reconcile (baseline: ____)
[ ] Rung 3: 3-5 rows hand-verified incl. edge cases
[ ] Rung 4: I can explain every clause and defend the grain
[ ] AI assistance disclosed where used
```

notes.title: Red lines: data, disclosure, and decisions
notes.body:
- RED LINE 1 — Sensitive data in prompts: never paste PII, credentials, or proprietary data into an AI tool unless your org has an approved, contracted arrangement. Assume prompts are logged.
- RED LINE 2 — Unverified outputs to stakeholders: an AI-drafted insight emailed without validation is your error, not the AI's. You signed it.
- RED LINE 3 — AI-written numbers without checks: narratives are fine to draft; NUMBERS must come from queries you ran and validated. Never let the AI invent a metric.
- Citation rule: if the AI cites a source for a factual claim, open the source yourself. If you can't find it, the claim doesn't ship.
- Career framing: 'I use AI tooling for drafting and debugging, with a strict validation workflow' is a senior answer. 'The AI said so' is a junior one.

```text
Pre-send gate for any AI-assisted deliverable:
1. Every number traces to a query I ran (not text the AI wrote).
2. Every factual claim has a source I opened myself.
3. No sensitive data was pasted into any AI tool to produce it.
4. AI assistance is disclosed to the recipient where material.
If any gate fails, the deliverable doesn't ship.
```

notes.title: What a data contract is (and isn't)
notes.body:
- A data contract is a documented, versioned agreement: 'the orders feed will contain these columns with these types and meanings, refreshed by 6 AM daily, owned by the checkout team, with 7 days notice before breaking changes.'
- It is NOT just a schema file. Schema says 'column amount is NUMERIC'; the contract adds semantics ('amount is in USD, refunds excluded'), freshness ('by 6 AM ET'), and ownership ('checkout-team@').
- Without a contract, every upstream change is a surprise: a renamed column breaks your mart at 7 AM and you find out from the stakeholder, not the producer.
- With a contract, breaking changes are announced, versioned, and migration-planned — the failure mode shifts from 'silent breakage' to 'scheduled migration'.

```yaml
# contract: orders feed v3 (example structure, adapt to your org's format)
contract: orders-feed
version: 3
owner: checkout-team@
schema:
  - {name: order_id, type: string, required: true}
  - {name: amount, type: numeric, required: true,
     semantics: 'USD, refunds excluded; see refunds table'}
  - {name: order_date, type: date, required: true}
freshness: {sla: '06:00 ET daily', late_policy: 'page owner after 30 min'}
change_policy: {breaking_notice_days: 7, channel: '#data-contracts'}
```

notes.title: Schema vs semantics: the two halves
notes.body:
- Schema contract: names, types, nullability, allowed values. Machine-checkable — this is what becomes dbt tests and pipeline assertions.
- Semantic contract: what the fields MEAN. 'amount' excluding refunds vs including them is a semantic difference no type checker catches — and it's the difference between a right and wrong revenue number.
- The analyst's job: when a number looks off, check semantics first ('did the definition of active_user change?'), schema second.
- Document semantics where the data is consumed (dbt column descriptions, semantic layer definitions) — a contract nobody can find is decoration.

```yaml
# The same schema, two different semantics -> two different revenues
columns:
  - name: amount
    tests: [not_null]
    description: >-
      SEMANTICS (contract v3): USD gross merchandise value at order time,
      refunds EXCLUDED (see refunds table), tax included. Changed 2026-09-01:
      previously included refunds. Historical comparison must note the break.
```

```sql
-- A semantic change the schema can't catch: definition of 'active'
-- Contract v2: active = logged in within 30d. Contract v3: within 7d.
-- Your dashboard drops 40% overnight with zero schema change.
-- Fix: version the metric definition, annotate the break, never silently splice.
```

notes.title: From contract to enforcement: tests and monitors
notes.body:
- Every contract clause becomes something executable: schema -> dbt generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values); freshness SLA -> a recency monitor ('max(order_date) older than 26h -> alert'); change policy -> CI check that diffs the contract file.
- Consumer-side: your staging models assert the contract on ingest — fail fast at the boundary instead of propagating bad data into marts.
- Versioning: contracts are versioned (v3), and consumers pin to a version. The producer supports v2 and v3 during the migration window, then retires v2 per the notice policy.
- Escalation path in the contract: who gets paged, in what channel, with what severity — agreed BEFORE the 6 AM failure, not during it.

```sql
-- tests/freshness_orders.sql: contract SLA as a singular test (0 rows = fresh)
SELECT MAX(order_date) AS latest
FROM {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
HAVING MAX(order_date) < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
-- Violation rows -> the 06:00 ET SLA from the contract is breached.
```

notes.title: Negotiating a contract: what analysts should demand
notes.body:
- Ask for: explicit nullability per column, allowed-value sets for codes/statuses, the freshness SLA in writing, a named owner (team + channel), and the breaking-change notice period.
- Concede gracefully: you can't demand real-time from a batch source; negotiate the SLA you actually need ('6 AM is fine; what I need is the page when it's late').
- Bring evidence: 'last quarter, three silent schema changes cost us two dashboard incidents' beats 'contracts are best practice'.
- Review cadence: contracts rot. Reconfirm semantics quarterly for your top-5 critical feeds — definitions drift even when schemas don't.

```text
Analyst's contract request (template):
1. Schema: column names/types/nullability + allowed values for codes.
2. Semantics: one-line definition per business-critical field.
3. Freshness: SLA timestamp + late-notification channel.
4. Ownership: team + on-call channel.
5. Change policy: notice period for breaking vs additive changes.
6. Versioning: contract version pinned by consumers; migration window.
Send this to the producer team; track the response like any dependency.
```

notes.title: The metric-sprawl problem
notes.body:
- Without a semantic layer: Sales defines revenue as 'bookings including tax', Finance as 'recognized excluding refunds', and the exec dashboard shows a third number — three 'revenues', zero trust.
- Root cause: metric logic lives inside individual dashboards and notebooks, copied and subtly mutated each time.
- A semantic layer centralizes definitions: each metric is defined ONCE (name, logic, grain, owner) and every consumer — dashboard, notebook, AI assistant — queries the definition, not a copy.
- The payoff is trust: 'revenue' means the same everywhere, and when the definition changes, it changes everywhere at once, with an owner and a changelog.

```yaml
# metrics/revenue.yml — defined once, consumed everywhere
metric: revenue
definition:
  measure: order_amount_sum        # SUM(amount) over the orders mart
  filters: [amount >= 0]           # refunds excluded, per contract v3
  time_grain: day
  dimensions: [region, channel, product_category]
owner: finance-analytics
description: 'USD gross merchandise value, refunds excluded, tax included.'
status: certified
```

notes.title: Dimensions, measures, metrics: the vocabulary
notes.body:
- Dimension: an attribute you slice by — region, channel, date. Answers 'by what?'.
- Measure: an aggregation over a fact — SUM(amount), COUNT(orders). Answers 'how much?' — but a raw measure has no business rules yet.
- Metric: a measure + business logic + governance — filters (exclude refunds), grain (daily), definition, owner, certification status. 'Revenue' is a metric; SUM(amount) is a measure.
- Grain discipline: a metric must declare its grain ('one row per day per region'). Comparing a daily metric to a monthly one without alignment is the classic apples-to-oranges error.

```yaml
# measure vs metric: the business logic is what makes it a metric
measures:
  - name: order_amount_sum
    agg: sum
    expr: amount            # raw aggregation, no rules

metrics:
  - name: revenue
    measure: order_amount_sum
    filters: [amount >= 0]  # the business rule lives HERE
    # grain: day  (declared, so consumers can't mis-aggregate)
```

```sql
-- What the layer compiles 'revenue by region, last 30d' into:
SELECT region, DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date) AS day, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM marts.orders
WHERE amount >= 0 AND order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY region, day
```

notes.title: One definition, many consumers
notes.body:
- The same metric definition serves: BI dashboards (the tool queries the layer, not raw tables), notebooks (analysts import certified metrics instead of rewriting logic), and AI assistants (the AI grounds 'revenue' in the defined metric instead of guessing SQL).
- This is the AI-safety payoff from Module 47: an AI that answers 'what was revenue?' through the semantic layer can't invent its own definition — it inherits the certified one.
- Consistency check: pick any metric, query it from two consumers, compare. Divergence means someone bypassed the layer — treat it as an incident, not a curiosity.
- Migration path: don't boil the ocean. Start with your 5 most-disputed metrics, certify them, point the exec dashboard at the layer, expand.

```python
# notebook consumer: certified metric, not rewritten logic
from semantic_layer import metrics
rev = metrics.query('revenue',
                    dimensions=['region'],
                    date_range='last_30d')
# rev is computed from the certified definition — identical to the dashboard's.
```

notes.title: Governance: certification, ownership, deprecation
notes.body:
- Every metric has an owner (team/person) and a status: draft, certified, deprecated. Only certified metrics appear in the exec layer.
- Certification bar: definition reviewed, logic tested (dbt-style tests on the underlying model), semantics documented, stakeholder sign-off.
- Deprecation, not deletion: when 'revenue_v1' is replaced, mark it deprecated with a pointer to v2 and a sunset date — dashboards migrate on a schedule, nothing vanishes overnight.
- Naming discipline: one name, one meaning. 'Revenue' can't also mean 'net revenue' somewhere else — that's net_revenue, a different certified metric.

```yaml
# lifecycle in the metric registry
metric: revenue_v1
status: deprecated
replaced_by: revenue_v2
sunset_date: 2027-01-31
migration_note: 'v2 excludes tax per Finance sign-off 2026-11-15.'
# dashboards on v1 get a migration ticket, not a surprise.
```
