notes.title: XML anatomy: elements, attributes, namespaces
notes.body:
- XML is a tree: elements nest (`<order><id>1</id></order>`), attributes annotate (`<order priority="high">`), one root element per document.
- Well-formed (syntax: tags closed, nested properly) vs valid (conforms to a schema like XSD) — a file can be well-formed but invalid; parsing needs the first, contracts need the second.
- Namespaces (`xmlns:inv="..."`) prevent tag collisions when documents mix vocabularies — `<inv:total>` vs `<tax:total>`. They are the #1 reason XPath queries 'return nothing'.
- Analyst rule: always inspect the raw XML (first 50 lines) before writing any extraction — structure surprises (nested vs flat, attributes vs elements) are the norm.

```xml
<!-- orders.xml: elements carry data, attributes annotate -->
<orders xmlns="urn:il26:orders">
  <order id="1001" priority="high">
    <customer>Acme Corp</customer>
    <total currency="USD">250.00</total>
  </order>
  <order id="1002" priority="normal">
    <customer>Globex</customer>
    <total currency="USD">89.50</total>
  </order>
</orders>
```

notes.title: XPath: SQL for trees
XSLT: transform XML into something usable
notes.body:
- XSLT is a template language that transforms XML -> XML, HTML, or plain text (including CSV). Legacy pipelines use it to reshape feeds before analysts ever see them.
- You won't write stylesheets daily, but you must READ them: when a feed arrives 'wrong', the XSLT in the middle is often the culprit.
- Core: `<xsl:template match="...">` (which nodes), `<xsl:for-each>` (loop), `<xsl:value-of select="..."/>` (extract).
- Modern analyst move: skip XSLT when you can — parse the XML directly in Python (next note). Reach for XSLT when the transform must live in the pipeline, not your script.

```xml
<!-- orders-to-csv.xsl: flatten orders to CSV lines -->
<xsl:stylesheet version="1.0"
  xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"
  xmlns:o="urn:il26:orders">
  <xsl:output method="text"/>
  <xsl:template match="/">
    <xsl:text>order_id,customer,total
</xsl:text>
    <xsl:for-each select="//o:order">
      <xsl:value-of select="@id"/><xsl:text>,</xsl:text>
      <xsl:value-of select="o:customer"/><xsl:text>,</xsl:text>
      <xsl:value-of select="o:total"/><xsl:text>
</xsl:text>
    </xsl:for-each>
  </xsl:template>
</xsl:stylesheet>
<!-- output: order_id,customer,total / 1001,Acme Corp,250.00 / ... -->
```

notes.title: Python: XML to dataframe without silent loss
notes.body:
- ElementTree (stdlib) handles most feeds; lxml when you need full XPath or broken-HTML tolerance.
- Pattern: iterate record elements, extract fields with namespace-aware finds, build a list of dicts, DataFrame it.
- Namespace handling in ElementTree: use the Clark notation `{urn:il26:orders}order` or register a prefix map — pick one and be consistent.
- Malformed XML: parse defensively — catch ParseError, log the offending file, quarantine it. A parser that silently skips records is worse than one that loudly fails.

```python
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
import pandas as pd

NS = {'o': 'urn:il26:orders'}
records = []
try:
    root = ET.parse('orders.xml').getroot()
    for o in root.findall('o:order', NS):
        records.append({
            'order_id': o.get('id'),                       # attribute
            'priority': o.get('priority', 'normal'),       # default if missing
            'customer': o.findtext('o:customer', '', NS),   # element text
            'total': float(o.findtext('o:total', '0', NS)),
            'currency': o.find('o:total', NS).get('currency'),
        })
except ET.ParseError as e:
    raise SystemExit(f'QUARANTINE orders.xml: malformed ({e}) — fix source, do not silently skip')

df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(df, df['total'].sum())
```

**Analyst's notebook: how this topic shows up in real data work.**

*XML, XPath, and XSLT for Data Analysts* earns its keep when a stakeholder asks a question the dashboard can't answer. The professional pattern is always the same: clarify the business question first, check the data's fitness second, do the analysis third — never the reverse.

- **The question behind the question.** 'Can you pull the numbers?' usually means 'help me decide X'. Get the decision on the table before touching data.
- **Garbage in, gospel out.** No amount of modeling fixes mislabeled, duplicated, or stale source data. Profile the data before analyzing it.
- **One chart, one message.** If a visualization needs a paragraph to explain, redesign it. The takeaway should survive a three-second glance.
- **Show your work.** Assumptions, filters, and exclusions belong in the deliverable, not in your head. Reproducibility is what separates analysis from opinion.
- **Answer, then caveat.** Lead with the finding and its confidence; put methodology and limitations after, not before.

Bring this discipline to Read XML documents: elements, attributes, namespaces, and well-formedness rules; Write XPath expressions to select nodes, filter by predicates, and extract values — stakeholders remember analysts who answer the real question, not the asked one.

notes.title: Narrative arc: SCR (Situation-Complication-Resolution)
notes.body:
- Situation: shared context everyone agrees on ('Q3 revenue was $4.2M, up 8%').
- Complication: the tension that demands a decision ('...but churn in the West region doubled, erasing the gain').
- Resolution: your recommendation ('Reallocate $200K of acquisition spend to West retention; projected +$600K net').
- The arc turns a data dump into a story with stakes. Executives decide; they don't explore — your deck must arrive at the decision, not invite wandering.
- Test: cover the slide headlines only — they should read as a coherent paragraph. If they don't, the story is broken.

```text
Headline-only test (the deck's story in 5 lines):
1. Q3 revenue grew 8% to $4.2M           (situation)
2. But West-region churn doubled, erasing the gain  (complication)
3. Churn concentrates in customers acquired via discount codes (insight)
4. We recommend shifting $200K to West retention   (resolution)
5. Projected net: +$600K; decision needed by Friday (ask)
```

notes.title: One message per slide: headline = takeaway
notes.body:
- Rule: the slide title states the CONCLUSION ('West churn doubled in Q3'), not the topic ('Churn analysis'). The visual below is the evidence.
- One chart per slide, one takeaway per chart. Two messages = two slides.
- Annotate the chart: circle the spike, label the key value, add the 'so what' in a caption. Never make the audience hunt for the point.
- Data-ink discipline: remove gridlines, 3D effects, and decoration that doesn't encode information. If removing an element changes nothing, remove it.

```text
BEFORE (topic title):  "Churn by region"  + busy 3D bar chart
AFTER (takeaway title): "West churn doubled in Q3, erasing the revenue gain"
                        + flat bars, West bar highlighted, annotation:
                          "2.1% -> 4.3% (n=1,204)"
The audience gets the message in 3 seconds, with or without you talking.
```

notes.title: Honest charts: the integrity checklist
notes.body:
- Baselines: bar charts start at zero — truncated bars exaggerate differences. (Line charts may zoom, but say so.)
- No dual axes with different scales unless you label both loudly — they manufacture correlations.
- Label directly: put values on the bars/points, not just on an axis the audience must interpolate.
- Show uncertainty: error bars or 'n=' counts where the data is thin. A 50% lift on n=12 is noise wearing a costume.
- Sourcing: every chart gets a source + date footnote ('orders mart, 2026-10-06'). Unsourced charts are rumors.
- The Module 47 rule applies: every number traces to a validated query.

```text
Chart integrity checklist (run per visual):
[ ] Bars start at zero (or zoom is disclosed)
[ ] No sneaky dual axes
[ ] Values labeled directly on the visual
[ ] n= shown; uncertainty visible where thin
[ ] Source + as-of date in the footnote
[ ] Number traces to a validated query (Module 47 ladder)
```

notes.title: Audience tailoring and the close
notes.body:
- Executives: BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front. Recommendation on slide 2, supporting evidence after, deep dive in the appendix. Never make them wait 20 slides for the point.
- Peers/technical: methodology earns slides — assumptions, grain, validation. They'll challenge the logic; arm them.
- The close: recommendation (one sentence), tradeoffs (what we give up), the ask (decision/resource/date), next steps with owners.
- Leave-behind: the deck must stand alone — headlines carry the story, appendix holds the proof, notes hold the narration you gave live.

```text
Closing slide template:
  RECOMMENDATION: Shift $200K acquisition -> West retention (Q4).
  TRADEOFF:      East acquisition growth slows ~3%.
  ASK:           Approve by Friday to hit the Q4 window.
  NEXT STEPS:    Ana: retention offer design (10/14) | Ben: spend reallocation (10/15)
  APPENDIX:      methodology, query logic, sensitivity analysis
```

**Problem.** Your deck has 20 slides of exploration and the recommendation appears on slide 19. The fix:
A. BLUF: recommendation on slide 2, evidence after, deep dive in appendix ←

**Walkthrough.**

2. Eliminate the distractors: B (Add 10 more slides); C (Make the recommendation smaller); D (It's fine) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).

notes.title: Analyst's notebook: PowerPoint Data Storytelling
notes.body:
**Analyst's notebook: how this topic shows up in real data work.**

*PowerPoint Data Storytelling* earns its keep when a stakeholder asks a question the dashboard can't answer. The professional pattern is always the same: clarify the business question first, check the data's fitness second, do the analysis third — never the reverse.

- **The question behind the question.** 'Can you pull the numbers?' usually means 'help me decide X'. Get the decision on the table before touching data.
- **Garbage in, gospel out.** No amount of modeling fixes mislabeled, duplicated, or stale source data. Profile the data before analyzing it.
- **One chart, one message.** If a visualization needs a paragraph to explain, redesign it. The takeaway should survive a three-second glance.
- **Show your work.** Assumptions, filters, and exclusions belong in the deliverable, not in your head. Reproducibility is what separates analysis from opinion.
- **Answer, then caveat.** Lead with the finding and its confidence; put methodology and limitations after, not before.

Bring this discipline to Structure a findings deck with a narrative arc: situation, complication, resolution, recommendation; Apply one-message-per-slide: headline as the takeaway, visual as the evidence — stakeholders remember analysts who answer the real question, not the asked one.

objectives: Structure a findings deck with a narrative arc: situation, complication, resolution, recommendation
Apply one-message-per-slide: headline as the takeaway, visual as the evidence
Design honest charts: proper baselines, labeled axes, no truncated or dual-axis deception
Tailor the deck to the audience: executive summary up front, appendix for the deep dive
Deliver with the decision in mind: recommendation, tradeoffs, ask, and next steps on the final slides

objectives: Compute mean, median, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules of probability.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Data Analyst
notes.body:
**Relevance.** The entire analyst craft — distributions, hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, regression — is statistics. This module is the mathematical core of the certificate.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Describing data: center and spread
notes.body: For data x₁..xₙ: the mean x̄ = (Σxᵢ)/n; the median is the middle value when sorted; the variance s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1) (sample) and standard deviation s = √s². Worked example (verified): response times [12, 15, 13, 90, 14] ms. Mean = (12+15+13+90+14)/5 = 144/5 = 28.8. Median: sorted [12,13,14,15,90] → 14. The single outlier (90) drags the mean to 28.8 while the median stays 14 — this is why latency is reported with medians/percentiles, not means. Deviations from mean: [−16.8, −13.8, −15.8, 61.2, −14.8]; squared sum = 282.24+190.44+249.64+3745.44+219.04 = 4686.8; sample variance = 4686.8/4 = 1171.7; s ≈ 34.2 ms. Report center AND spread together — a mean without spread is a half-truth.

notes.title: Probability rules that never change
notes.body: Sample space S, event A: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1. Addition rule: P(A∪b) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) (subtract the double-counted overlap); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0. Complement: P(not A) = 1−P(A). Multiplication: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(B|A)=P(B). Worked example (verified): a queue has 30% high-priority tickets (H) and 20% are escalations (E); 12% are both. P(H∪E) = 0.30+0.20−0.12 = 0.38. If instead H and E were independent, P(both) would be 0.30×0.20 = 0.06 ≠ 0.12 — so they are NOT independent (escalations skew high-priority). Two independent deploys each fail with p=0.05: P(both fail) = 0.05² = 0.0025; P(at least one fails) = 1−(0.95)² = 1−0.9025 = 0.0975.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
notes.body: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B): probability of A given B occurred. Bayes inverts the conditioning: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+). Worked example — alert triage (verified): 1% of hosts are compromised (P(D)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of compromised hosts (sensitivity P(+|D)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of clean hosts (P(+|¬D)=0.05). P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099+0.0495 = 0.0594. P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 ≈ 0.1667 — only ~16.7%! Most alerts are false positives despite a "99% accurate" detector, because the base rate is tiny. This base-rate effect is the single most important probability lesson for SOC triage, medical screening, and fraud detection: accuracy without the base rate is meaningless. Always expand P(+) via total probability before trusting a positive.

notes.title: Expectation and variance of random variables
notes.body: For discrete X with values xᵢ and probabilities pᵢ: E[X] = Σxᵢpᵢ (long-run average); Var(X) = E[X²]−(E[X])²; SD = √Var. Linearity: E[aX+b] = aE[X]+b, and E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when dependent. Worked example — fair die (verified): E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. E[X²] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.1667. Var = 91/6 − 3.5² = 15.1667−12.25 = 2.9167 = 35/12. SD ≈ 1.708. Worked example 2: a Bernoulli trial with success p has E[X]=p and Var=p(1−p) — variance peaks at p=0.5 (maximum uncertainty). In ML, cross-entropy loss is minimized exactly when predicted probabilities match these expectations; in capacity planning, E[load] sizes the average but Var(load) sizes the headroom.

notes.title: The binomial and normal distributions
notes.body: Binomial(n,p): number of successes in n independent trials; P(X=k) = C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p). Normal(μ,σ²): the bell curve; the 68-95-99.7 rule says P(|X−μ|<σ)≈0.68, <2σ ≈0.95, <3σ ≈0.997. Worked example — binomial (verified): 5 independent alert rules, each fires spuriously with p=0.3. P(exactly 2 fire) = C(5,2)·0.3²·0.7³ = 10×0.09×0.343 = 0.3087 ≈ 30.9%. Worked example — normal: API latency ~ Normal(μ=120ms, σ=15ms). P(latency > 150) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.0228 — about 2.3% of requests. The Central Limit Theorem is why the normal appears everywhere: averages of many small independent effects are approximately normal, which justifies z-intervals for A/B test readouts and poll margins.

notes.title: Hypothesis testing and confidence, honestly
notes.body: A hypothesis test asks: "is this data surprising under the null hypothesis H₀?" The p-value is P(data this extreme | H₀) — NOT P(H₀ is true). Reject H₀ when p < α (often 0.05). A 95% confidence interval is a procedure that covers the true parameter in 95% of repetitions — not "95% chance the truth is inside this interval". Worked example (verified): conversion rate baseline 10% (H₀: p=0.10). In n=400 trials we observe 52 conversions (ς=0.13). SE = √(0.1×0.9/400) = √(0.000225) = 0.015. z = (0.13−0.10)/0.015 = 2.0. Two-sided p ≈ 0.0455 < 0.05 — reject H₀; the lift is statistically significant. But "significant" ≠ important: a 3-point lift may not cover the feature’s cost. Report effect size and confidence interval alongside every p-value, pre-register the hypothesis (no p-hacking), and remember that with 20 metrics tested, one will be "significant" by chance alone.

cards.back: Mean = Σx/n (pulled by outliers: [12,15,13,90,14] → 28.8); median = middle value (14) — robust.
s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1); standard deviation s = √s².
P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Subtract the overlap; mutually exclusive ⇒ last term 0.
P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(B|A) = P(B).
P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+), with P(+) expanded by total probability.
With 1% prevalence and 5% false-alarm rate, P(compromised|alert) ≈ 16.7% — most alerts are false.

cards.back: C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k); E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p).
For Normal(μ,σ): ≈68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of μ.
P(data this extreme | H₀) — not P(H₀ true). Reject H₀ when p < α.

cards.back: SE=0.015, z=2.0, two-sided p≈0.0455 — significant at α=0.05.

handsOnLab.title: Verify probability by simulation with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify the Bayes triage calculation, the binomial probability, and the die variance three ways: by hand formula, by exact computation, and by Monte Carlo simulation. All three must agree.
steps: Open python3. Simulate the Bayes scenario: 1M hosts, 1% compromised; detector: 99% sensitivity, 5% false-alarm. Count positives and the fraction compromised among them; confirm ≈0.167.
Compute exactly: (0.99*0.01)/(0.99*0.01+0.05*0.99). Compare with the simulation to 3 decimals.
Binomial check: from math import comb; compute comb(5,2)*0.3**2*0.7**3; then simulate 200k runs of 5 Bernoulli(0.3) trials and compare the fraction with exactly 2 successes.
Die variance: exact = sum(x*x for x in range(1,7))/6 - 3.5**2; simulate 500k die rolls, compute sample variance; compare.
Break it: change prevalence to 50% in the Bayes simulation and watch P(D|+) jump — record both values to feel the base-rate effect.
Write up: the three agreements (formula vs exact vs simulation) and one sentence on why simulation is a legitimate verification tool.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up with the three verified numbers (Bayes ≈0.1667, binomial ≈0.3087, die variance ≈2.9167) from all three methods.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Simulation, exact computation, and hand formula agree to 2+ decimals on all three quantities.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Linear Algebra for Data Analyst
modules.summary: Vectors, dot products, matrices and multiplication, inverses, linear systems, and eigenvalues — the geometry of embeddings, attention, and least-squares fitting. Prerequisite spine for Data Analyst.
objectives: Add, scale, and dot vectors; compute norms and projections.
Multiply matrices and verify results by hand.
Invert 2×2 matrices and solve linear systems.
Compute eigenvalues of 2×2 matrices via the characteristic polynomial.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Data Analyst
notes.body:
**Relevance.** PCA, embeddings, and least-squares regression are linear algebra. This module gives you the geometry behind the techniques.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Vectors: addition, scaling, dot product
notes.body: A vector v in R^n is an n-tuple; add componentwise, scale by multiplying each component. The dot product u·v = Σuᵢvᵢ measures alignment: positive when pointing the same way, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposed. Worked example (verified): u=(1,2,3), v=(4,−1,2). u+v = (5,1,5). 2u = (2,4,6). u·v = 1·4 + 2×(−1) + 3×2 = 4−2+6 = 8. Since 8 > 0, the angle between them is acute. In embeddings and attention, dot products ARE similarity scores: softmax(QK^T) is a matrix of scaled dot products deciding what each token attends to. Orthogonal vectors (dot 0) represent unrelated directions — the geometric meaning of "uncorrelated features".

notes.title: Norms, unit vectors, and projections
notes.body: The Euclidean norm ||v|| = √(v·v) is the vector’s length. A unit vector has norm 1; normalize via v/||v||. The projection of u onto v is ((u·v)/(v·v))v — the shadow of u along v. Worked example (verified): v=(3,4). ||v|| = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. Unit vector: (3/5, 4/5) = (0.6, 0.8); check: 0.36+0.64=1 ✓. Projection of u=(1,2) onto v: u·v = 3+8 = 11; v·v = 25; proj = (11/25)(3,4) = (33/25, 44/25) = (1.32, 1.76). Cosine similarity = (u·v)/(||u||·||v||) = 11/(√5×5) = 11/11.18 ≈ 0.984 — nearly parallel. Normalization is why cosine similarity (not raw dot) compares embedding directions fairly: it divides out magnitude.

notes.title: Matrices and matrix multiplication
notes.body: An m×n matrix has m rows, n columns. (AB)ᵢⱼ = row i of A dotted with column j of B; A (m×n) times B (n×p) gives m×p. Worked example (verified): A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]]. AB[1,1] = 1·5+2×7 = 5+14 = 19. AB[1,2] = 1·6+2×8 = 6+16 = 22. AB[2,1] = 3·5+4×7 = 15+28 = 43. AB[2,2] = 3·6+4×8 = 18+32 = 50. So AB = [[19,22],[43,50]]. Check BA = [[5+18, 10+24],[7+24, 14+32]] = [[23,34],[31,46]] ≠ AB — multiplication does NOT commute. Every neural-network layer is x → Wx+b: a matrix multiply plus bias. The non-commutativity is why layer ORDER matters.

notes.title: Identity, transpose, and inverses
notes.body: I has 1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere; AI = A. Transpose A^T flips rows/columns: (AB)^T = B^T A^T. A is invertible if some A^−1 satisfies AA^−1 = I; for 2×2 [[a,b],[c,d]] with det = ad−bc ≠ 0, the inverse is (1/det)[[d,−b],[−c,a]]. Worked example (verified): A=[[2,1],[1,1]]. det = 2×1−1×1 = 1. A^−1 = [[1,−1],[−1,2]]. Verify: [[2,1],[1,1]]×[[1,−1],[−1,2]] = [[2−1, −2+2],[1−1, −1+2]] = [[1,0],[0,1]] ✓. If det = 0 the matrix is singular — it crushes some direction to zero (no inverse). In least squares, X^TX must be invertible; a zero determinant means perfectly collinear features (redundant columns), and the fix is regularization or dropping a feature.

notes.title: Solving linear systems
notes.body: Ax = b asks: which combination of A’s columns equals b? For small systems, elimination works: add multiples of equations to kill variables. Worked example (verified): 2x+y = 5 and x−y = 1. Add the equations: 3x = 6 ⇒ x = 2. Substitute: 2−y = 1 ⇒ y = 1. Check: 2(2)+1 = 5 ✓, 2−1 = 1 ✓. Matrix form: [[2,1],[1,−1]][x,y]^T = [5,1]^T; x = A^−1 b with A^−1 = (−1/3)[[−1,−1],[−1,2]] = [[1/3,1/3],[1/3,−2/3]]; x = (5+1)/3 = 2, y = (5−2)/3 = 1 ✓. Geometrically each equation is a line; the solution is their intersection. No intersection (parallel lines) = inconsistent; infinite intersections = dependent equations. Gaussian elimination is this process systematized — O(n³), the cost behind every "solve" call.

notes.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
notes.body: Av = λv: v is an eigenvector if A only scales it (by eigenvalue λ). Solve det(A−λI) = 0, the characteristic polynomial. Worked example (verified): A=[[4,1],[2,3]]. A−λI = [[4−λ,1],[2,3−λ]]. det = (4−λ)(3−λ)−2 = 12−7λ+λ²−2 = λ²−7λ+10 = (λ−5)(λ−2). Eigenvalues: λ=5 and λ=2. Eigenvector for λ=5: [[−1,1],[2,−2]][x,y]^T=0 ⇒ −x+y=0 ⇒ v=(1,1). Check: A(1,1) = (5,5) = 5(1,1) ✓. Eigenvalues reveal a matrix’s action: the largest dominates long-run behavior (PageRank, power iteration), and PCA keeps the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalues — the directions of maximum variance.

cards.back: 4−2+6 = 8 (positive ⇒ acute angle).
[[19,22],[43,50]] — row·column each entry.
[[1,−1],[−1,2]] (det=1). Verified by multiplication to I.
det = 0 — it crushes some direction to zero; no inverse exists.
λ²−7λ+10=0 ⇒ λ=5, 2. Eigenvector for 5: (1,1).
Nonzero v with Av=λv — A only scales it.
(u·v)/(||u||·||v||) — dot product with magnitudes divided out.
((u·v)/(v·v))v — the shadow of u along v.

handsOnLab.brief: You will verify every hand computation in these notes with NumPy: dot products, norms, matrix multiplication, inverses, system solving, and eigenvalues. The machine must reproduce your numbers exactly.

Multiply A=[[1,2],[3,4]] by B=[[5,6],[7,8]] with A@B; assert the result equals [[19,22],[43,50]]. Confirm A@B != B@A.
Invert [[2,1],[1,1]] with np.linalg.inv; assert it equals [[1,-1],[-1,2]]; multiply back to get the identity.
Solve the system with np.linalg.solve([[2,1],[1,-1]],[5,1]); assert [2.0, 1.0].
Eigenvalues: np.linalg.eigvals([[4,1],[2,3]]); assert sorted values are [2.0, 5.0]. Verify A@v == 5*v for v=[1,1].
Write up: which checks passed, and one sentence on why machine verification complements (never replaces) hand computation.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up listing each NumPy verification and its agreement with the hand-computed notes.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All six NumPy checks reproduce the notes’ numbers exactly.

mockTask.q: Your embedding pipeline ranks documents by dot product with the query vector, but long documents always win. The principled fix?
choices: Normalize vectors and use cosine similarity
mockTask.explain: Raw dot products confound direction with magnitude. Cosine similarity divides out norms, comparing directions fairly.

questions.q: A retailer keeps raw clickstream files for two years, then deletes them under a documented retention policy. Which phase of the data life cycle does the deletion belong to?
choices: Destroy, because the data is removed at the end of its useful life
Manage, because storage costs are being optimized
Archive, because the old data is kept offline
Capture, because new data collection has stopped
questions.explain: Destroy is the life-cycle phase where data that has served its purpose is removed according to policy.

questions.q: Which choice correctly lists the FAIR data principles?
questions.explain: FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.

questions.q: A dataset of 50 million rows and 200 columns is described as having high variety and velocity. Which two big-data Vs are missing from that description?
questions.explain: The five Vs are volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value; volume and veracity are the ones not named.

questions.q: In a tidy dataset, each variable forms a column, each observation forms a row, and each value sits in a single cell. Which data shape does this describe?
questions.explain: The variable-per-column, observation-per-row layout is the tidy (long) format.

questions.q: A table's column names, data types, owner, and last-refresh date are examples of what?
choices: Metadata, because they describe the data itself
Primary keys, because they identify each row
Aggregates, because they summarize the table
Schemas, because they define the database engine
questions.explain: Metadata is data about data, such as definitions, lineage, and refresh information.

questions.q: A marketing manager asks: 'Increase email open rates by 10 percent within two quarters by testing subject lines.' Which statement about this objective is true?
choices: It is not measurable because open rates fluctuate
It is a SMART objective: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound
It is a business task, not an objective
It fails SMART because two quarters is too vague
questions.explain: It names a specific metric, a target, a method, and a deadline, satisfying all five SMART criteria.

questions.q: A data analyst is asked to cut churn, but the requester cannot say which customers are churning or why. What is the best first step?
choices: Ask clarifying questions to define the problem and the decisions the analysis will inform
questions.explain: The Ask phase requires turning a vague request into a defined problem with stakeholders, scope, and decisions.

questions.q: Grouping customer support tickets into topics like billing, shipping, and returns is an example of which problem type?
questions.explain: Assigning items to defined groups based on shared features is the categorizing-things problem type.

questions.q: A scope of work for an analysis engagement should define which of the following?
choices: Deliverables, timeline, milestones, and reporting expectations
The exact SQL queries to be written
The analyst's job title and salary
questions.explain: A scope of work sets shared expectations on deliverables, schedule, milestones, and communication.

questions.q: An analyst notices the survey data underrepresents rural customers, who behave differently. What is the fairest next step before modeling?
choices: Drop the rural responses to keep the data clean
Oversample or reweight to represent rural customers, and document the limitation
Proceed, since the sample is large enough
Replace rural responses with urban averages
questions.explain: Fairness means identifying representation gaps, correcting for them where possible, and disclosing remaining limits.

questions.q: Two CSV files list orders and customers. Both contain a customer_id column. Which join keeps only rows with a match in both files?
questions.explain: An inner join returns only rows whose key exists in both tables.

questions.q: An analyst receives weekly sales extracts where dates appear as 'Jan 3', '01/03', and '3-Jan'. Before analysis, the dates must be converted to one consistent type. Which data quality issue is this?
questions.explain: Mixed representations of the same values are a consistency (data type/format) issue to fix in preparation.

questions.q: Which practice best protects the credibility of collected data?
choices: Documenting sources, collection methods, and any transformations applied
Deleting raw files once analysis starts
Keeping the methodology secret from stakeholders
Collecting as much data as possible without a plan
questions.explain: Documented lineage lets others verify how the data was gathered and changed.

questions.q: In SQL, which keyword removes duplicate rows from a result set?
questions.explain: SELECT DISTINCT returns only unique combinations of the selected columns.

questions.q: A wide table stores one column per month (Jan_Sales ... Dec_Sales). To plot monthly trends, the analyst reshapes it so months become rows. This operation is called what?
questions.explain: Converting month columns into month rows is a wide-to-long (unpivoting) reshape.

questions.q: A product column mixes 'CA', 'Calif.', and 'California'. Converting all values to 'CA' is an example of what cleaning step?
questions.explain: Mapping variant spellings to one canonical value is standardization.

questions.q: Which spreadsheet function removes leading and trailing spaces from text?
questions.explain: TRIM strips extra spaces from text, a common first cleaning step.

questions.q: Checking a cleaned dataset against a trusted reference source to confirm values are correct is called what?
questions.explain: Verification compares data to an authoritative source to confirm correctness.

questions.q: An analyst must clean the same messy extract every Monday. Which approach is most reproducible?
choices: A version-controlled script or notebook that reruns the same steps
Asking a colleague to eyeball it
questions.explain: Scripted, versioned cleaning steps rerun identically and leave an audit trail.

questions.q: In SQL, how does AVG() treat NULL values in a column?
choices: It ignores NULLs in the calculation
It returns NULL if any value is NULL
questions.explain: Aggregate functions like AVG skip NULLs rather than treating them as zero.

questions.q: What does SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY region return?
choices: One row per region with the number of orders in that region
The total number of orders overall
One row per order with its region
The distinct regions with no counts
questions.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per region, and COUNT(*) tallies the rows in each group.

questions.q: An analyst finds a correlation of -0.85 between ticket price and units sold. What does this suggest?
choices: Higher prices cause exactly 85 percent fewer sales
A strong negative association: as price rises, units sold tend to fall
No relationship between price and sales
Price and sales move up together
questions.explain: A correlation near -1 indicates a strong inverse linear association, not proof of causation.

questions.q: Which SQL clause filters the results AFTER aggregation?
questions.explain: HAVING filters grouped/aggregated rows; WHERE filters rows before aggregation.

questions.q: Sorting products by revenue descending and keeping the first 10 rows is an example of what?
questions.explain: Ordering by a metric and taking the top N is a ranking analysis.

questions.q: In analysis, 'pivoting' data most directly enables which of the following?
choices: Viewing the same data summarized across different dimensions
questions.explain: A pivot reorganizes data so it can be summarized across rows, columns, and filters.

questions.q: Which chart best compares the share of five product categories when exact proportions matter?
choices: A bar chart showing each category's percentage
questions.explain: Bar charts encode values by length, making precise comparison easier than angled pie slices.

questions.q: A line chart is the most appropriate choice for which of the following?
choices: Comparing categories at one point in time
questions.explain: Line charts connect ordered time points to reveal trends and seasonality.

questions.q: Which principle best helps an analyst reduce chartjunk?
choices: Use a rainbow palette for all series
Maximize the data-ink ratio by removing non-essential decoration
Include every available metric on one chart
questions.explain: A high data-ink ratio means most ink carries data, not decoration.

questions.q: An effective chart title should do what?
choices: State the takeaway message, not just the topic
List the data source in small print
questions.explain: Takeaway titles tell the audience what the chart proves, guiding interpretation.

questions.q: What is the most important design rule for an executive dashboard?
choices: Fit every available chart on one screen
Limit the view to the key metrics that drive decisions
Use a different color scheme per chart
Refresh data only once per quarter
questions.explain: Dashboards serve decisions; each view should carry only the metrics that inform them.

questions.q: In R, which operator pipes the output of one function into the next?
questions.explain: The magrittr pipe %>% (and base R's |>) passes a result forward as the next function's input.

questions.q: Which dplyr verb keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition?
questions.explain: filter() subsets rows by a logical condition; select() picks columns.

questions.q: What does ggplot(sales, aes(x = month, y = revenue)) + geom_col() produce?
choices: A column chart of revenue by month
A scatter plot of month vs revenue
questions.explain: geom_col() draws bars with heights taken directly from the y values.

questions.q: Which function reads a CSV file into an R data frame?
questions.explain: Base R's read.csv() and readr's read_csv() both parse CSVs into data frames/tibbles.

questions.q: To compute the mean revenue per region in dplyr, which combination is correct?
questions.explain: group_by(region) followed by summarize(mean = mean(revenue)) aggregates within each group.

questions.q: What is the best first step when starting a capstone case study?
choices: Open the data and start charting
Clarify the business question, stakeholders, and success criteria
questions.explain: Capstones are judged on problem framing first; analysis without a defined question wanders.

questions.q: Which evidence most strongly supports a capstone recommendation?
choices: Results that hold across multiple cuts and checks of the data
Agreement with the stakeholder's prior belief
questions.explain: Robustness across segments, time windows, and methods makes a finding trustworthy.

questions.q: Including one optional deeper analysis beyond the brief demonstrates what to a reviewer?
choices: Curiosity and ownership of the problem
questions.explain: A well-chosen extra cut shows initiative, as long as the core deliverable is complete.

questions.q: When presenting capstone findings to executives, what should come first?
choices: The recommendation and its expected business impact
A tour of every chart produced
questions.explain: Executives decide on recommendations; lead with the answer, then support it.

questions.q: A complete capstone portfolio piece includes which of the following?
choices: The raw data files with no explanation
The business question, process, visuals, and recommendation
questions.explain: Reviewers look for end-to-end thinking: framing, method, evidence, and a decision-ready conclusion.
