toolLabs.title: Python: Load and Clean the Sample Dataset
toolLabs.brief: The chain starts here: load the fictional ecom_orders CSV in pandas, profile it, clean it (types, nulls, dedupe), and save a cleaned Parquet that every later lab builds on. This cleaned file is the single source of truth for the whole chain.
steps: Create the project folder il26-tool-chain/ and save the ecom_orders dataset as data/raw/ecom_orders.csv
Write clean_orders.py: read the CSV with pandas, print shape, dtypes, and null counts per column
Convert order_date to datetime, amount to numeric; strip whitespace and uppercase region/channel/category values
Deduplicate on order_id (keep first, log how many duplicates were found — expect zero, prove it)
Treat empty discount_code as 'NONE'; assert no negative amounts and no null order_ids (raise if violated)
Write the result to data/clean/ecom_orders_clean.parquet; print final row count and a 5-row sample
Commit clean_orders.py and the row-count log to git with message 'TL-01: cleaned orders baseline'
toolLabs.deliverable: data/clean/ecom_orders_clean.parquet plus clean_orders.py committed to git
toolLabs.checkpoint: Re-running clean_orders.py produces the identical Parquet (same row count, same checksum); the script raises loudly on any failed assertion instead of silently passing bad data.

toolLabs.title: SQL: Model It in DuckDB
toolLabs.brief: Move the cleaning logic from Python into SQL: create a persistent DuckDB database, define typed tables with constraints, and re-implement TL-01's cleaning as SQL transformations — the same dataset, now modeled the analytics-engineering way.
steps: Create analytics.duckdb and a raw schema: CREATE TABLE raw.orders AS FROM read_csv('data/raw/ecom_orders.csv', header=true)
Run data-quality checks in SQL: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), COUNT(amount) — record the baseline numbers
CREATE TABLE clean.orders AS SELECT with explicit CASTs: order_date::DATE, amount::DECIMAL(10,2), UPPER(TRIM(region))
Implement the TL-01 rules in SQL: COALESCE(NULLIF(discount_code,''), 'NONE'), dedupe with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id)
Add a date dimension table clean.dim_date (date, year, month, quarter, day_of_week) generated with generate_series
Build clean.orders_daily: one row per date with orders, revenue, avg_order — the mart the BI labs will consume
Verify parity: the DuckDB clean.orders row count and revenue total EXACTLY match the TL-01 Parquet (document both numbers)
toolLabs.deliverable: analytics.duckdb with raw.orders, clean.orders, clean.dim_date, clean.orders_daily, plus parity numbers vs TL-01
toolLabs.checkpoint: SELECT COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) from clean.orders match the TL-01 Parquet totals exactly; clean.orders_daily has one row per date with no gaps.

toolLabs.title: dbt: Models, Tests, and Docs from the SQL Layer
toolLabs.brief: Convert the TL-02 SQL into a real dbt project: staging models, a daily mart, data tests on every rule from TL-01/TL-02, and generated docs with lineage. Same logic, now versioned, tested, and documented.
steps: dbt init il26_chain --adapter duckdb; point profiles.yml at your analytics.duckdb file
Declare the source: raw orders CSV in models/sources.yml (source 'raw', table 'orders')
Write models/staging/stg_orders.sql: the TL-02 cleaning SELECT with {{ source('raw','orders') }}
Write models/marts/orders_daily.sql: the daily grain mart with {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
Add schema YAML: not_null + unique on order_id, relationships on customer_id, accepted_values on region/channel
Add singular tests: no_negative_amounts.sql and no_future_order_dates.sql (each must return 0 rows)
Run dbt build until green; then dbt docs generate and screenshot the lineage graph for your portfolio

toolLabs.checkpoint: dbt build exits 0 with all tests passing; dbt docs shows stg_orders -> orders_daily lineage; orders_daily totals match TL-02's mart exactly.

toolLabs.title: Tableau: Dashboard from the Modeled Data

Write DAX measures: Total Revenue = SUM(orders_daily[revenue]), Total Orders, Avg Order Value = DIVIDE([Total Revenue],[Total Orders])

Compute the 3 KPIs with formulas: =SUM(amount_range), =COUNTA(order_id_range), =AVERAGE(amount_range)
Build a pivot table: rows = region, values = Sum of amount and Count of order_id; add channel as a slicer
Build a second pivot: rows = order_date grouped by month, values = Sum of amount (the monthly trend)

Sidebar controls: region multiselect, channel multiselect, date-range slider — all filters combine

multicloudLabs.title: AWS: S3 + Athena Query on the Sample Orders CSV
multicloudLabs.brief: Run one real analytics workload on AWS's free tier: upload the fictional ecom_orders CSV to S3, query it with Athena's serverless SQL engine (pay-per-query, no servers), then tear everything down. You will touch a bucket, a table definition, and a query — and leave no billable residue.
steps: Sign in to the AWS console and choose a region close to you (e.g. us-east-1); do ALL work in this one region so resources are easy to find at cleanup
Create an S3 bucket with a globally unique name (e.g. il26-lab-<yourname>-<date>); keep Block Public Access ON and versioning OFF
Upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv to the bucket under s3://<bucket>/raw/ecom_orders.csv
Open Athena, run the one-time setup: set the query-result location to s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ (Athena needs a place to write results)

In the Athena query editor, create the table: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE orders (order_id string, order_date string, customer_id string, region string, channel string, product_category string, amount double, discount_code string) ROW FORMAT DELIMITED FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' STORED AS TEXTFILE LOCATION 's3://<bucket>/raw/' TBLPROPERTIES ('skip.header.line.count'='1')
Run the workload query: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC — confirm it matches your local DuckDB totals
Check the Athena query history panel: note the 'Data scanned' amount for your queries (this is what Athena bills on — small CSV means fractions of a cent)
multicloudLabs.workload: Athena serverless SQL over the S3-hosted ecom_orders CSV: revenue and order counts by region, reconciled against the local DuckDB totals from TL-02. The workload demonstrates decoupled storage (S3) and serverless compute (Athena) — the core cloud analytics pattern.
costGuardrails: Athena's free tier covers a small monthly query-data allowance; a 15-row CSV scans kilobytes — stay on tiny files and this lab costs essentially nothing
S3 free tier covers a small amount of storage and requests monthly; one CSV plus query results is far below it — do not upload large datasets
Keep everything in ONE region; cross-region data movement is where surprise charges come from
Do not enable S3 versioning, replication, or intelligent-tiering on the lab bucket — all add cost for zero lab benefit
Set a billing alert (e.g. $1) in the Billing console before starting — the habit matters more than the threshold
cleanup: Athena: no persistent compute to delete (serverless), but note your query history for the report
S3: delete s3://<bucket>/athena-results/ contents, then s3://<bucket>/raw/ecom_orders.csv, then delete the bucket itself
Verify: S3 console shows zero buckets matching il26-lab-*; Billing dashboard shows no active resources
Record the final 'Data scanned' totals and confirm the month-to-date bill is $0.00 before closing the lab
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Athena query results match local DuckDB region totals exactly; lab bucket deleted; billing dashboard shows $0.00; 'Data scanned' recorded.

multicloudLabs.title: Azure: Storage + Synapse Serverless SQL on the Sample Orders CSV
multicloudLabs.brief: Run the same workload on Azure: land the fictional ecom_orders CSV in Azure Storage and query it with Synapse's serverless SQL pool (pay per terabyte scanned, no cluster to manage). Free-account framing throughout, full teardown at the end.
steps: Sign in to the Azure portal; confirm you are on a free account/trial subscription and note its expiry date before creating anything
Create a resource group named il26-lab-rg in a region near you — everything goes here so cleanup is one deletion
Create a Storage account (standard performance, LRS redundancy — the cheapest options) inside il26-lab-rg
In the storage account, create a container named raw and upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv

Open Synapse Studio, create a serverless SQL pool workspace (or use an existing one), and run: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(CAST(amount AS FLOAT)),2) AS revenue FROM OPENROWSET(BULK 'https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/raw/ecom_orders.csv', FORMAT='CSV', PARSER_VERSION='2.0', HEADER_ROW=TRUE) AS o GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC
Reconcile the results against your local DuckDB totals — same numbers, different cloud
Check the Synapse monitoring view: note the data processed by the query (this is the billing meter)
multicloudLabs.workload: Synapse serverless SQL over the Storage-hosted ecom_orders CSV via OPENROWSET: revenue and order counts by region, reconciled against local DuckDB totals. Demonstrates Azure's decoupled storage-plus-serverless-query pattern, the direct analog of the AWS lab.
costGuardrails: Serverless SQL pools bill per terabyte of data processed; a 15-row CSV processes megabytes — keep files tiny and queries few
Free accounts include limited monthly credits: this lab uses a negligible fraction, but never run ad-hoc exploratory queries against large files on a free account
Use the cheapest storage options (standard, LRS) — premium tiers and geo-redundancy multiply cost for no lab benefit
Do NOT provision a dedicated SQL pool or Spark pool — those bill per hour while running and are unnecessary for this workload
Put everything in the single il26-lab-rg resource group so nothing billable hides outside it
cleanup: Delete the entire resource group il26-lab-rg (this removes the storage account, container, and any Synapse artifacts in one action)
Verify: portal search for il26-lab-rg returns nothing; storage accounts list shows no lab account
Check Cost Management: confirm the subscription shows no ongoing charges from the lab resources
Record the data-processed totals from Synapse monitoring for your lab report
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Query results match local DuckDB totals; resource group il26-lab-rg deleted and verified gone; Cost Management shows no ongoing lab charges.

multicloudLabs.title: GCP: BigQuery Sandbox Query on the Sample Orders Dataset
multicloudLabs.brief: Run the workload on Google Cloud's BigQuery sandbox — which lets you query without even adding a billing account. Load the fictional ecom_orders CSV, run the regional revenue analysis, and clean up the dataset. The sandbox's limits ARE the guardrails here.
steps: Sign in to the Google Cloud console and create/select a project named il26-lab; open BigQuery Studio
Confirm you are in sandbox mode (no billing account attached — the console labels it); note the sandbox's table expiration behavior before loading data
Create a dataset named lab_orders in a US region; upload data/raw/ecom_orders.csv as a table named orders (auto-detect schema, header row = 1)
Run the workload query: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS revenue FROM `il26-lab.lab_orders.orders` GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC
Reconcile against local DuckDB totals; then run one variant: monthly revenue trend with DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)
Open the query job details: note bytes processed and slot time — this is what BigQuery meters
multicloudLabs.workload: BigQuery SQL over the uploaded ecom_orders table: regional revenue/orders plus a monthly trend, reconciled against local DuckDB totals. Demonstrates the warehouse-native pattern (data loaded INTO the engine) as contrast to the S3/Storage query-in-place pattern of the other two labs.
costGuardrails: The BigQuery sandbox requires no billing account and grants a monthly free query allowance — but sandbox tables EXPIRE (default 60 days) and some features are restricted; know these limits before relying on sandbox data

With billing enabled later, BigQuery's free tier covers a monthly query-data allowance — the 15-row table processes kilobytes; never point ad-hoc queries at multi-terabyte public datasets on a free tier without checking bytes-processed first
Always check the query validator's 'bytes processed' estimate BEFORE running — it is displayed in the editor and is your pre-flight cost check
Keep the lab to the two queries specified; exploratory querying against large tables is the classic free-tier-burn mistake
cleanup: Delete the lab_orders dataset (deleting the dataset removes the orders table with it)
Verify: BigQuery explorer shows no lab_orders dataset under il26-lab
Optionally delete the il26-lab project itself for a fully clean slate
Record bytes-processed totals from both query jobs for your lab report
multicloudLabs.checkpoint: Both queries' results match local DuckDB totals; lab_orders dataset deleted and verified gone; bytes-processed recorded for both jobs.

steps: Open the Python downloads page at https://www.python.org/downloads/ and click the yellow "Download Python 3.12.x" button (take the newest 3.12 or 3.13 point release).

Run the downloaded .exe. On the FIRST installer screen, check the box labeled "Add python.exe to PATH" at the very bottom — this is the step most beginners miss, and skipping it breaks every later tool.
Click "Install Now" and let the installer finish. Accept the prompt to disable the MAX_PATH length limit if it appears.
Close and reopen your terminal (or PowerShell), then run the verification checkpoints below.
windows.notes: If you installed without the PATH box checked, uninstall and reinstall — fixing PATH by hand is slower than a clean reinstall.

steps: Open https://www.python.org/downloads/ and click "Download Python 3.12.x" to get the macOS 64-bit installer (.pkg).
Run the .pkg and accept the defaults through the wizard.
After install, open the Applications > Python 3.12 folder and double-click "Install Certificates.command" so pip can download packages over HTTPS.
Open Terminal and run the verification checkpoints below. macOS ships its own old Python; always call python3/pip3, not python/pip.
Open a terminal. On Ubuntu/Debian run: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv
On Fedora/RHEL run: sudo dnf install -y python3 python3-pip
Confirm with the checkpoints below. If your distro ships an older Python 3, add the deadsnakes PPA (Ubuntu) or use the official tarball rather than building from source.

checkpoints.expected: Python 3.12.x (or newer, e.g. 3.13.x)
pip 24.x from ... (python 3.12)

troubleshoot.symptom: Windows: 'python' is not recognized as an internal or external command
troubleshoot.fix: You skipped the Add-to-PATH checkbox. Reinstall and check it on the first screen, or run the installer again and choose Modify > add python.exe to PATH.

troubleshoot.symptom: Windows: typing python opens the Microsoft Store
troubleshoot.fix: That is the fake app-execution alias. Either turn off the alias in Settings > Apps > Advanced app settings > App execution aliases, or just use py -3 instead of python everywhere.

troubleshoot.symptom: macOS: pip install fails with SSL certificate errors
troubleshoot.fix: You skipped Install Certificates.command. Run it from Applications > Python 3.12, then retry pip.

troubleshoot.symptom: Linux: 'externally-managed-environment' error on pip install
troubleshoot.fix: Your distro protects system Python. Install packages into a virtualenv instead: python3 -m venv ~/venv && source ~/venv/bin/activate, then pip install.

installLabs.costNote: Free and open source forever. Python has no paid tier and no expiry.

steps: Open https://git-scm.com/download and let the page pick the Windows installer for you (click "Click here to download").
Run the installer. On the PATH screen choose "Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software" (the recommended middle option).
On the line-ending screen choose "Checkout Windows-style, commit Unix-style line endings".
On the terminal emulator screen choose "Use Windows' default console window" unless you have a reason not to.
Finish the install, open a NEW terminal, and run the checkpoints.
The simplest route: install Apple's command line tools by running xcode-select --install in Terminal and accepting the prompt — Git comes with them.
Alternatively install Homebrew from https://brew.sh, then run brew install git.
Run the checkpoints to confirm.
Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git
Fedora/RHEL: sudo dnf install -y git
Run the checkpoints, then set your identity: git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "your@email.com" — commits are rejected by most hosts without these.

checkpoints.expected: git version 2.4x.x (any recent 2.x)
Your name, as you configured it (non-empty)

troubleshoot.symptom: Windows: 'git' is not recognized in a new terminal
troubleshoot.fix: The installer PATH option was set to Git Bash only. Reinstall and choose "Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software".

troubleshoot.symptom: macOS: xcode-select --install says tools already installed but git missing
troubleshoot.fix: Reset with sudo xcode-select --reset then run xcode-select --install again, or fall back to brew install git.

troubleshoot.symptom: Push asks for a password and your GitHub password does not work
troubleshoot.fix: GitHub removed password auth years ago. Create a personal access token (GitHub Settings > Developer settings > Tokens) and use it as the password, or set up SSH keys.

installLabs.costNote: Free and open source forever. Git itself costs nothing; hosting accounts (GitHub, GitLab) have free tiers generous enough for a portfolio.

steps: Open https://code.visualstudio.com/download and download the Windows User Installer (64-bit).
Run the installer. On the "Select Additional Tasks" screen, check "Add to PATH" and "Add 'Open with Code' action to Windows Explorer context menus" — both save real time later.
Launch VS Code, open the Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X), and install the "Python" extension by Microsoft and the "Jupyter" extension by Microsoft. These power the Python and notebook tool-labs.
In a terminal run the checkpoints below.
Open https://code.visualstudio.com/download and download the macOS build (choose Apple Silicon if your Mac has an M1/M2/M3/M4 chip, Intel otherwise).
Open the .zip, drag Visual Studio Code into Applications, and launch it.
Press Cmd+Shift+P, type "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH", and run it so the code command works in Terminal.
Install the Microsoft Python and Jupyter extensions from the Extensions panel (Cmd+Shift+X).
Ubuntu/Debian: download the .deb from https://code.visualstudio.com/download and run sudo apt install ./code_*.deb (it adds Microsoft's repo so updates arrive automatically).
Fedora/RHEL: download the .rpm and run sudo dnf install ./code-*.rpm.
Launch with the code command, then install the Microsoft Python and Jupyter extensions.

checkpoints.expected: 1.9x.x followed by a commit hash line (any recent 1.x)

troubleshoot.symptom: 'code' command not found after install
troubleshoot.fix: Windows: reinstall with "Add to PATH" checked. macOS: run the "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" palette command. Linux: log out and back in so the PATH change takes effect.

troubleshoot.symptom: Python files do not run or show no interpreter
troubleshoot.fix: Install the Microsoft Python extension, then press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac) and run "Python: Select Interpreter" to point at your Python 3.12+ install.

troubleshoot.symptom: Jupyter notebooks show "No kernel"
troubleshoot.fix: Install the Microsoft Jupyter extension and the ipykernel package: pip install ipykernel, then restart VS Code.

installLabs.costNote: Free forever for individuals. VS Code has no paid tier; the marketplace extensions used in this course are all free.

steps: Confirm Python 3.12+ is installed (finish IL26-INST-01 first).
In a terminal run: pip install notebook jupyterlab
Launch with: jupyter lab — your browser should open to the JupyterLab interface automatically. If it does not, copy the http://localhost:8888/... URL printed in the terminal into your browser.
To stop the server, press Ctrl+C in the terminal and confirm shutdown.
windows.notes: If pip warns about scripts not on PATH, add %APPDATA%\Python\Python312\Scripts to your user PATH.

steps: Confirm Python 3.12+ is installed (finish IL26-INST-01 first).
In Terminal run: pip3 install notebook jupyterlab
Launch with: jupyter lab — your browser opens automatically. Create a test notebook, run print("hello"), and confirm output appears.
Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
Confirm Python 3.12+ and pip are installed (finish IL26-INST-01 first).
Create a virtualenv to dodge the externally-managed-environment error: python3 -m venv ~/jupyter-env && source ~/jupyter-env/bin/activate
Run: pip install notebook jupyterlab, then jupyter lab. Open the printed URL if the browser does not launch.
Stop with Ctrl+C; reactivate the env with source ~/jupyter-env/bin/activate next session.

checkpoints.expected: jupyter_core ... / notebook ... / jupyterlab ... (version lines for the installed packages)

troubleshoot.symptom: 'jupyter' is not recognized after pip install
troubleshoot.fix: The Scripts/bin directory is not on PATH. Reinstall Python with Add-to-PATH (Windows) or add ~/.local/bin to PATH (macOS/Linux): export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH".

troubleshoot.symptom: Notebook kernel dies immediately on start
troubleshoot.fix: Install the kernel package explicitly: pip install ipykernel, then in Jupyter choose Kernel > Change kernel > Python 3.

troubleshoot.symptom: Port 8888 already in use
troubleshoot.fix: Another server is running. Launch with jupyter lab --port 8889 instead.

installLabs.costNote: Free and open source forever. Jupyter runs locally on your machine; no account, no cloud bill.

steps: Open https://dbeaver.io/download/ and download the Windows 64-bit installer (the .exe, not the zip).
Run the installer with defaults — it bundles its own Java runtime, so you do not need to install Java separately.
Launch DBeaver. On first run it asks to create a sample database; you can decline — you will connect to PostgreSQL/MySQL from later labs.
Open a new connection wizard (Database > New Database Connection) and confirm the driver list loads; drivers download on first use, which requires internet.
Open https://dbeaver.io/download/ and download the macOS .dmg (Apple Silicon build if you have an M-series Mac).
Open the .dmg, drag DBeaver into Applications, and launch it. If macOS blocks it, right-click > Open to approve the unsigned developer once.
Decline the sample database on first run and confirm the new-connection wizard loads its driver list.
Ubuntu/Debian: download the .deb from https://dbeaver.io/download/ and run sudo apt install ./dbeaver-ce_*.deb
Fedora/RHEL: download the .rpm and run sudo dnf install ./dbeaver-ce-*.rpm
Launch with dbeaver-ce and confirm the new-connection wizard loads its driver list.

checkpoints.command: Open DBeaver > Help > About (or DBeaver > About DBeaver on macOS)
checkpoints.expected: DBeaver Community Edition, version 24.x or newer

troubleshoot.symptom: Driver download fails when creating a connection
troubleshoot.fix: You need internet on first use per driver. Check DBeaver > Preferences > Connections > Drivers > Maven to change the artifact repository if your network blocks the default.

troubleshoot.symptom: macOS: app is damaged / cannot be opened
troubleshoot.fix: Run xattr -cr /Applications/DBeaver.app in Terminal to strip the quarantine attribute, then launch again.

troubleshoot.symptom: OutOfMemoryError on large result sets
troubleshoot.fix: Raise the heap in dbeaver.ini (-Xmx1024m to -Xmx4096m) — Community Edition defaults are conservative.

installLabs.costNote: Community Edition is free and open source forever. The paid Pro/Ultimate editions add cloud and NoSQL features the course does not require.

steps: Open https://www.postgresql.org/download/ , choose Windows, and download the interactive installer from EDB for PostgreSQL 16.
Run the installer. WRITE DOWN the superuser (postgres) password you set — you will need it for every local connection.
Keep the default port 5432 and default locale. On the component screen you can uncheck Stack Builder; keep pgAdmin if you want a web GUI, or skip it since DBeaver covers that role.
After install, open SQL Shell (psql) from the Start menu, press Enter through the defaults, type your postgres password, and run SELECT version(); to confirm.
windows.notes: The EDB installer is the beginner-safe path on Windows; the zip archive is for advanced users only.

steps: Install Homebrew from https://brew.sh if you do not have it, then run: brew install postgresql@16
Start the service: brew services start postgresql@16
Create your user role: createuser -s $(whoami) — then you can connect without a password over the local socket.
Verify with: psql -c "SELECT version();"
macos.notes: Postgres.app is a fine GUI alternative, but the Homebrew route matches the checkpoints and keeps one package manager for everything.

steps: Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-contrib
Start and enable it: sudo systemctl start postgresql && sudo systemctl enable postgresql
Switch to the postgres user to create your role: sudo -u postgres createuser -s $USER, then create your database: sudo -u postgres createdb $USER
Verify with: psql -c "SELECT version();" — with no password prompt, since local peer auth trusts your OS user.

checkpoints.expected: PostgreSQL 16.x ... (a version string mentioning 16)

troubleshoot.symptom: psql: could not connect to server — connection refused
troubleshoot.fix: The service is not running. Windows: start the postgresql-x64-16 service in Services. macOS: brew services restart postgresql@16. Linux: sudo systemctl start postgresql.

troubleshoot.symptom: password authentication failed for user postgres
troubleshoot.fix: You mistyped the superuser password from install time. Windows: rerun the EDB installer and reset it. Linux/macOS socket users: connect as your OS user instead of postgres.

troubleshoot.symptom: role "yourname" does not exist
troubleshoot.fix: Create the role first: as the postgres superuser run CREATE ROLE yourname WITH LOGIN SUPERUSER; then reconnect.

troubleshoot.symptom: Port 5432 already in use during install
troubleshoot.fix: Another Postgres (or Docker container) holds the port. Stop the other instance or install on port 5433 and note it for connection strings.

installLabs.costNote: Free and open source forever. Local PostgreSQL costs nothing and never expires; managed cloud Postgres (RDS, Cloud SQL) is a separate paid product you do not need here.

steps: Open https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/installer/ and download the MySQL Installer for Windows (the larger ~500 MB bundle includes the server; the small web installer downloads components during setup).
Run the installer, choose the "Developer Default" setup type, and walk through the server configuration screens.
On the Accounts and Roles screen, WRITE DOWN the root password you set. On the Windows Service screen keep "Start the MySQL Server at System Startup" checked.
Finish, then open MySQL Shell or the legacy Command Line Client from the Start menu, log in as root, and run SELECT VERSION(); to confirm.
Install Homebrew from https://brew.sh if needed, then run: brew install mysql
Start the service: brew services start mysql
Secure it: mysql_secure_installation — set a root password when prompted (WRITE IT DOWN), and accept the suggested hardening answers.
Verify with: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT VERSION();" (type the root password at the prompt).
Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y mysql-server
Start and enable: sudo systemctl start mysql && sudo systemctl enable mysql
Run sudo mysql_secure_installation to set a root password and apply the hardening steps.
Verify with: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT VERSION();"

checkpoints.expected: mysql  Ver 8.0.x ... (an 8.0 version string)

troubleshoot.symptom: Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'
troubleshoot.fix: Wrong root password. On Linux, sudo mysql lets the OS root in without a password — use that to reset: ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'newpassword';

troubleshoot.symptom: Can't connect to MySQL server on 'localhost' (10061 / 2002)
troubleshoot.fix: The service is not running. Windows: start MySQL80 in Services. macOS: brew services restart mysql. Linux: sudo systemctl start mysql.

troubleshoot.symptom: MySQL Workbench or DBeaver connects but immediately disconnects
troubleshoot.fix: Check that the server's bind-address allows localhost and that no second MySQL/MariaDB instance is fighting over port 3306.

installLabs.costNote: MySQL Community Server is free under the GPL forever. The paid Enterprise edition is a separate product the course never requires.

steps: The Python route is fastest: with Python 3.12+ installed run pip install duckdb
For the standalone CLI, open https://duckdb.org/docs/installation/ , download the Windows 64-bit zip, and unzip duckdb.exe somewhere on your PATH (e.g. a folder you add to user PATH).
Verify both with the checkpoints below.
Python route: pip3 install duckdb
CLI route: brew install duckdb — this gives you the duckdb shell command.
Verify with the checkpoints below.
Python route: pip install duckdb (use a virtualenv if your distro enforces externally-managed-environment).
CLI route: download the Linux binary from https://duckdb.org/docs/installation/ , unzip, and move duckdb to /usr/local/bin or ~/bin on your PATH.
Verify with the checkpoints below.

checkpoints.expected: 1.x.x (a version number like 1.1.3)

troubleshoot.symptom: pip install duckdb fails to build
troubleshoot.fix: Use a prebuilt wheel instead of building: upgrade pip first (pip install --upgrade pip) and retry — DuckDB ships wheels for all major platforms, so a build attempt means pip is too old to find them.

troubleshoot.symptom: duckdb CLI: command not found after unzipping
troubleshoot.fix: The binary is not on PATH. Either move it to a PATH directory or call it by its full path.

troubleshoot.symptom: Out of memory on a big CSV read
troubleshoot.fix: DuckDB is in-process and shares your RAM. Read in chunks, add a LIMIT while exploring, or set PRAGMA memory_limit to a safe value.

installLabs.costNote: Free and open source (MIT license) forever. DuckDB is an embedded analytical database — no server, no account, no expiry.

steps: Create a free Tableau account at https://public.tableau.com/en-us/s/download if you do not have one (email + password, confirm the verification email).
On the same page, download Tableau Public Desktop for Windows and run the installer with defaults.
Launch Tableau Public and sign in with your new account.

Open a sample: connect to the built-in "Sample - Superstore" data source, drag Sales to Columns and Profit to Rows, and confirm a chart renders — you will save workbooks to your public profile in the tool-labs.
windows.notes: Tableau Public saves ONLY to your public Tableau profile — anything you publish is visible to everyone. Never use real client or employer data here.

steps: Create a free Tableau account at https://public.tableau.com/en-us/s/download (confirm the verification email).
Download Tableau Public Desktop for macOS, open the .dmg, and drag it to Applications.
Launch, sign in, and build the quick Sample - Superstore test chart described above.
macos.notes: Tableau Public saves ONLY to your public Tableau profile — keep all practice data fictional or public.

linux.notes: Tableau Public Desktop has no Linux build. Use the Tableau Public web authoring at https://public.tableau.com in a browser to complete the Tableau Public tool-labs, or run the Windows build in a VM.

checkpoints.command: Open Tableau Public > Help > About Tableau
checkpoints.expected: Tableau Public, version 2024.x or newer, and you are signed in (your profile name shows in the top bar)

troubleshoot.symptom: Installer fails with a .NET or WebView2 error on Windows
troubleshoot.fix: Tableau needs Microsoft Edge WebView2. Install it from Microsoft's WebView2 download page, reboot, and rerun the Tableau installer.

troubleshoot.symptom: Sign-in loops back to the login screen
troubleshoot.fix: Clear the app's cached credentials: sign out inside Tableau, close it fully, reopen, and sign in again. Corporate SSO blockers can also interfere — use a personal email account.

troubleshoot.symptom: Cannot save a workbook locally
troubleshoot.fix: That is by design in Tableau Public — saving uploads to your public profile. If you need private local files, you need Tableau Desktop (IL26-INST-10).

installLabs.costNote: Free forever. The tradeoff is privacy: every workbook you save is public on the internet. The paid Tableau Desktop/Creator license is not required for this course.

steps: Open https://www.tableau.com/products/desktop/download and start the free trial — you will create a Tableau account with your email.
Download the Windows 64-bit installer and run it with defaults.
Launch Tableau Desktop and activate the trial with your account when prompted (the trial clock starts at activation, so activate only when you are ready to do the Desktop tool-labs).
Connect to Sample - Superstore, build one sheet, and save the .twbx locally to confirm private saving works.
windows.notes: Do not activate until you are ready to work the Desktop labs — the 14-day clock cannot be paused.

steps: Open https://www.tableau.com/products/desktop/download and start the free trial with your email.
Download the macOS installer (.dmg), drag to Applications, launch, and activate the trial.
Build and locally save one Sample - Superstore sheet to confirm private saving.
macos.notes: Same warning: activate only when you plan to use it; the trial is 14 days.

linux.notes: Tableau Desktop has no Linux build. Complete the Desktop tool-labs via Tableau Cloud trial in a browser, or use a Windows/macOS machine or VM.

checkpoints.command: Open Tableau Desktop > Help > About Tableau
checkpoints.expected: Tableau Desktop 2024.x or newer, showing trial days remaining

troubleshoot.symptom: Trial activation says the product key is invalid
troubleshoot.fix: Trials activate through account sign-in, not a typed key. Make sure you are signing in with the same email you used to start the trial.

troubleshoot.symptom: Trial expired before you finished the labs
troubleshoot.fix: Tableau grants one trial per email. The Tableau Public lab (IL26-INST-09) covers most Desktop skills; use Public for remaining practice, keeping data fictional.

troubleshoot.symptom: Installer blocked by antivirus
troubleshoot.fix: Temporarily allow the installer in your AV's quarantine list — the official installer from tableau.com is signed. Re-enable protection after install.

installLabs.costNote: 14-day free trial of Tableau Creator/Desktop. When it expires the app locks until you buy a license; Tableau Public (IL26-INST-09) stays free and covers most visualization skills.

steps: Open https://www.tableau.com/products/prep/download and start the free trial with your email (same account as Desktop if you have one).
Download the Windows 64-bit installer and run it with defaults.
Launch Tableau Prep Builder and activate the trial at the sign-in prompt — again, the clock starts at activation, so time it with the Prep tool-labs.
Open the built-in Superstore sample flow, run it, and confirm the output preview renders.
windows.notes: Prep Builder and Desktop trials are usually bundled under one Creator trial — activating one may start both clocks.

steps: Open https://www.tableau.com/products/prep/download , start the trial, download the macOS .dmg, and install to Applications.
Launch, activate, and run the sample Superstore flow to confirm.

linux.notes: Tableau Prep Builder has no Linux build. Cover the data-prep tool-lab concepts with the browser-based flow authoring in a Tableau Cloud trial, or use a Windows/macOS machine.

checkpoints.command: Open Tableau Prep Builder > Help > About
checkpoints.expected: Tableau Prep Builder 2024.x or newer, showing trial days remaining

troubleshoot.symptom: Flows fail with a Java error on launch
troubleshoot.fix: Prep bundles its own runtime; a stale TEMP directory or aggressive antivirus usually causes this. Clear %TEMP% (Windows) or /tmp and relaunch.

troubleshoot.symptom: Cannot connect to a database from a flow
troubleshoot.fix: Prep needs the same JDBC/ODBC drivers as Desktop. Install the vendor driver (e.g. PostgreSQL JDBC) via the driver download page linked in Prep's connection dialog.

installLabs.costNote: 14-day free trial, typically bundled with the Tableau Creator/Desktop trial. After expiry, practice data-prep concepts in Tableau Public or with Python/pandas instead.

steps: Option A (recommended): open the Microsoft Store app, search "Power BI Desktop", and install — the Store version updates itself automatically.
Option B: open https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/download/details.aspx?id=58494 and download the PBIDesktopSetup_x64.exe installer.
Launch Power BI Desktop. Sign in with a Microsoft account (personal or work) to enable publishing; you can also work fully offline without signing in.
Click Get Data > Excel, load any small spreadsheet, and confirm the Data view shows your table — the tool-labs build from there.
windows.notes: Power BI Desktop itself is free. Publishing to the Power BI service requires a Pro/Premium license, but every course lab runs locally and free.

macos.notes: Power BI Desktop is Windows-only and Microsoft ships no macOS build. Alternatives: use the Power BI service in a browser at https://app.powerbi.com (import data and build reports there), run Windows in a VM (Parallels/UTM), or use the Microsoft Store version on a Windows machine. The PL-300 tool-labs note which steps differ in the web service.

linux.notes: Power BI Desktop is Windows-only with no Linux build. Use the Power BI service at https://app.powerbi.com in a browser, or a Windows VM. All data-modeling concepts transfer; only the local file workflow differs.

checkpoints.command: Open Power BI Desktop > File > Help > About
checkpoints.expected: Power BI Desktop, version 2.13x.x or newer (monthly releases)

troubleshoot.symptom: Installer fails with a WebView2 error
troubleshoot.fix: Install Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime from Microsoft's download page, then rerun the Power BI installer.

troubleshoot.symptom: 'We couldn't sign you in' loop
troubleshoot.fix: You can skip sign-in entirely for local labs — click the X on the sign-in prompt and work offline. Sign-in is only needed to publish to the service.

troubleshoot.symptom: DAX measure shows an error on refresh
troubleshoot.fix: This is a formula issue, not an install issue — but first confirm your data loaded: check Data view row counts before debugging the DAX.

troubleshoot.symptom: macOS/Linux learner cannot follow a Desktop-only step
troubleshoot.fix: Use the web-service alternative in the platform notes and flag the step in the course forum — the tool-labs mark Desktop-only steps explicitly.

installLabs.costNote: Power BI Desktop is free forever. Publishing/sharing via the Power BI service needs a paid Pro license (~$14/user/month) or Premium capacity — the course never requires publishing, so the free Desktop (or web service free tier) is enough.

installLabs.tool: Microsoft Excel (desktop + web) and Google Sheets

steps: DESKTOP: if you have Microsoft 365, open Excel from the Start menu and confirm File > Account shows you are licensed. No 365? Install the free Excel mobile/desktop trial from microsoft.com or use Excel for the web below.
WEB: sign in at https://www.office.com or office.com with a Microsoft account — Excel for the web is free and covers most course labs.
GOOGLE SHEETS: sign in at sheets.google.com with any Google account — no install needed.
In both, open a blank workbook, type numbers in A1:A5, put =SUM(A1:A5) in A6, and confirm the total calculates.
windows.notes: Excel for the web lacks Power Query's full desktop features — the M16 tool-labs flag which exercises need desktop Excel.

steps: DESKTOP: install Excel via a Microsoft 365 subscription (App Store or microsoft.com download).
WEB: use Excel for the web at office.com with a free Microsoft account as the no-cost path.
GOOGLE SHEETS: sheets.google.com with any Google account.
Run the same =SUM(A1:A5) smoke test in each.
There is no Linux desktop Excel. Use Excel for the web at office.com (free Microsoft account) for every Excel exercise.
GOOGLE SHEETS: sheets.google.com — the primary spreadsheet for Linux learners in this course.
Run the =SUM(A1:A5) smoke test in both.
linux.notes: LibreOffice Calc is a fine offline fallback, but formulas and pivot behavior differ — prefer the web apps for course fidelity.

checkpoints.command: In Excel or Sheets: enter 1..5 in A1:A5 and =SUM(A1:A5) in A6
checkpoints.expected: A6 displays 15

troubleshoot.symptom: Excel for the web: Power Query / Get Data options are missing
troubleshoot.fix: Expected — the web app has a reduced ribbon. The M16 labs mark desktop-only steps; do those on desktop Excel or substitute the Sheets QUERY function where the lab allows.

troubleshoot.symptom: Formula shows as text instead of calculating
troubleshoot.fix: The cell is formatted as Text. Change format to General, then re-enter the formula (press F2 then Enter).

troubleshoot.symptom: Microsoft 365 trial expired mid-course
troubleshoot.fix: Fall back to Excel for the web (free) plus Google Sheets — every M16 concept is covered across the two free tools.

installLabs.costNote: Google Sheets and Excel for the web are free forever. Desktop Excel requires a Microsoft 365 subscription (or one-time Office license); the course is fully completable on the free web apps.

steps: Install R FIRST: open https://cran.r-project.org/ , click Download R for Windows > base > Download R-4.x.x for Windows, and run the installer with defaults.
Then install RStudio: open https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/ , download the Windows installer, and run it with defaults.
Launch RStudio (not RGui). In the Console pane run: install.packages("tidyverse") — accept the offer to install to your personal library, and say yes to compiling if asked.

tasks.prompt: List each company and month with the natural log of users, so exponential growth plots as a straight line.
tasks.hint: Use the LN() function on the users column and alias it ln_users.

tasks.prompt: Compute the month-over-month growth factor per company: users divided by the prior month's users (use LAG).
tasks.starterSQL:
SELECT company, month, users
FROM growth_metrics;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT company, month,
  users / LAG(users) OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY month) AS growth_factor
FROM growth_metrics
ORDER BY company, month;
tasks.hint: LAG(users) OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY month) gives the prior month; the first month per company yields NULL.

tasks.prompt: Show companies with April users above 2000, with LOG10(users) for a log-scale chart axis.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT company, LOG10(users) AS log10_users
FROM growth_metrics
WHERE month = '2026-04' AND users > 2000
ORDER BY company;
tasks.hint: Filter month = '2026-04' and users > 2000; all three companies qualify.

tasks.prompt: Total sales per store: a summation over days, grouped by store.
tasks.starterSQL:
SELECT store, amount
FROM daily_sales;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT store, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM daily_sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;
tasks.hint: SUM(amount) with GROUP BY store gives Harbor 1930, Lakeshore 1355, Riverside 2540.

tasks.prompt: Grand total across all stores and days: the double summation.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUM(amount) AS grand_total
FROM daily_sales;
tasks.hint: Drop the GROUP BY to collapse everything to one row: 5825.

tasks.prompt: For each store, the sum of squared daily amounts: a building block of variance.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT store, SUM(amount * amount) AS sum_of_squares
FROM daily_sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;
tasks.hint: Square inside the SUM: SUM(amount * amount).

tasks.prompt: UNION: customers who are enterprise OR signed up in 2026-02, one row per customer.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise'
UNION
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE signup_month = '2026-02'
ORDER BY name;
tasks.hint: UNION deduplicates: 5 enterprise + 3 February signups - 1 overlap (Cara) = 7.

tasks.prompt: INTERSECT: customers who are BOTH enterprise AND signed up in 2026-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.hint: Only Cara satisfies both conditions.

tasks.prompt: EXCEPT: enterprise customers who did NOT sign up in 2026-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise'
EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE signup_month = '2026-02'
ORDER BY name;
tasks.hint: Removes Cara from the 5 enterprise customers: Ada, Fay, Ivy, Leo.

tasks.prompt: Average, minimum, and maximum salary per department.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT dept, salary FROM employee_comp;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT dept,
  AVG(salary) AS avg_salary,
  MIN(salary) AS min_salary,
  MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employee_comp
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
tasks.hint: AVG, MIN, MAX with GROUP BY dept.

tasks.prompt: Departments with more than 3 employees, with headcount.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employee_comp GROUP BY dept;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employee_comp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY dept;
tasks.hint: HAVING filters after grouping: Engineering (4) and Support (4).

tasks.prompt: The overall standard deviation of salary: one number describing spread.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee_comp;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT STDDEV(salary) AS salary_stddev
FROM employee_comp;
tasks.hint: STDDEV (or STDDEV_POP) aggregates the whole table to one row.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Discrete calculus: running totals and differences

tasks.prompt: Running total of temperature: a discrete integral, via a windowed SUM ordered by time.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts,
  SUM(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM sensor_readings
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) accumulates; the explicit frame makes the intent clear.

tasks.prompt: Hour-over-hour temperature change: a discrete derivative, via LAG.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts,
  temp_c - LAG(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) AS hourly_change
FROM sensor_readings
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: Subtract the LAG value; the first row has no prior reading so its change is NULL.

tasks.prompt: Flag the hours where temperature rose more than 1.0 degree versus the prior hour.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts, temp_c
FROM (
  SELECT reading_ts, temp_c,
    temp_c - LAG(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) AS chg
  FROM sensor_readings
) t
WHERE chg > 1.0
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: Compute the change in a subquery, then filter: 10:00 (+1.3), 11:00 (+1.8), 12:00 (+1.5).

tasks.prompt: Rank orders within each region by amount and return the top order per region.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT region, customer, amount FROM orders ORDER BY region, amount DESC;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT region, customer, amount
FROM (
  SELECT region, customer, amount,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
) t
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY region;
tasks.hint: RANK (not ROW_NUMBER) keeps ties: East has two orders at 5100, so 4 rows return.

tasks.prompt: Running total of amount per region, ordered by order date, with an explicit frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT region, order_date, amount FROM orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT region, order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY region, order_date;
tasks.hint: PARTITION BY region restarts the total per region; the frame clause states the window explicitly.

tasks.prompt: Month-over-month change per customer: aggregate to monthly totals in a CTE, then LAG.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT customer, amount FROM orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT customer, SUBSTRING(order_date, 1, 7) AS ym, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer, SUBSTRING(order_date, 1, 7)
),
lagged AS (
  SELECT customer, ym, total,
    LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ym) AS prev
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT customer, ym, total, total - prev AS mom_change
FROM lagged
WHERE prev IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY customer, ym;
tasks.hint: The CTE collapses to customer-months; LAG gives the prior month; 8 customer-months have a predecessor.

tasks.prompt: Customers whose lifetime total exceeds their region's average customer total (two CTEs).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT customer, region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer, region;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH cust_tot AS (
  SELECT customer, region, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer, region
),
region_avg AS (
  SELECT region, AVG(total) AS avg_total
  FROM cust_tot GROUP BY region
)
SELECT c.customer, c.region, c.total
FROM cust_tot c JOIN region_avg r ON c.region = r.region
WHERE c.total > r.avg_total
ORDER BY c.customer;
tasks.hint: Beta (West), Echo and Foxtrot (East), Gamma and Helios (Central) clear their regional averages.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Channel performance: rates and variability in SQL

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate and average revenue per channel.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, converted, revenue FROM site_sessions;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel,
  SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
  AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: A rate is a mean of 0/1 flags: SUM(converted)*1.0/COUNT(*).

tasks.prompt: Revenue variability per channel: standard deviation and maximum.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, AVG(revenue) FROM site_sessions GROUP BY channel;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel,
  STDDEV(revenue) AS revenue_stddev,
  MAX(revenue) AS max_revenue
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: STDDEV next to the mean tells you whether the average is stable or noisy.

tasks.prompt: Channels with at least 5 sessions and a conversion rate above 0.5.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, COUNT(*) FROM site_sessions GROUP BY channel;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel, SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 AND SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) > 0.5
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: HAVING filters groups: organic (3/5) and paid (3/5) qualify; referral has only 4 sessions.

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate and average minutes per variant, with each variant's lift versus the overall average rate.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, AVG(minutes) FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH rates AS (
  SELECT variant,
    SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
    AVG(minutes) AS avg_minutes
  FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant
)
SELECT variant, conv_rate, avg_minutes,
  conv_rate - AVG(conv_rate) OVER () AS lift_vs_avg
FROM rates
ORDER BY variant;
tasks.hint: AVG() OVER () with no partition computes the grand mean across the two variant rows.

tasks.prompt: Sample size per variant: are the arms balanced?
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, COUNT(*) FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT variant, COUNT(*) AS n_users
FROM ab_users
GROUP BY variant
ORDER BY variant;
tasks.hint: 6 and 6: balanced. Unbalanced arms are the first thing to check before trusting a readout.

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate by variant AND new-vs-returning segment: does the effect hold in both?
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, is_new, converted FROM ab_users;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT variant, is_new,
  SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
  COUNT(*) AS n
FROM ab_users
GROUP BY variant, is_new
ORDER BY is_new, variant;
tasks.hint: New users: 0.667 both arms (no effect). Returning: 0.333 vs 0.667 (effect concentrated here).

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Grain checks on a sales fact table

tasks.prompt: Revenue by category: qty * unit_price summed at fact grain.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, qty, unit_price FROM sales_lines;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT category, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS revenue
FROM sales_lines
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
tasks.hint: Multiply inside the SUM: Electronics 994, Tools 600, Accessories 139.86.

tasks.prompt: Grain violations: order_id + product pairs appearing more than once.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, product FROM sales_lines;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, product, COUNT(*) AS line_count
FROM sales_lines
GROUP BY order_id, product
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1003/Widget A and o1010/Gadget Y are double-counted: the fact grain is broken there.

tasks.prompt: Dimension sanity: distinct customers and distinct orders in one row.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_lines;
tasks.hint: 7 customers, 11 orders: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) measures dimension cardinality.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Staging cleanup: dedupe, clean, incremental filter

tasks.prompt: Deduplicate: one row per (user_id, event_ts, event_type), keeping the lowest event_id.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, event_type, amount
FROM (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, event_ts, event_type ORDER BY event_id) AS rn
  FROM stg_events
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY event_ts;
tasks.hint: Two duplicate pairs (e1/e3, e2/e10) collapse: 14 rows become 12.

tasks.prompt: Clean amounts: purchase events only, with NULL amounts replaced by 0.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events WHERE event_type = 'purchase';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, COALESCE(amount, 0) AS clean_amount
FROM stg_events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
ORDER BY event_id;
tasks.hint: COALESCE(amount, 0) handles the NULL on e5; views and the refund are excluded.

tasks.prompt: Incremental load: only events newer than the watermark 2026-09-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, event_ts
FROM stg_events
WHERE event_ts > '2026-09-02'
ORDER BY event_ts;
tasks.hint: The watermark excludes everything through 2026-09-02: 9 rows remain.

tasks.prompt: Monthly category totals: the year-month grain a Tableau extract would carry.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT txn_date, category, amount FROM retail_txns;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category,
  SUM(amount) AS total
FROM retail_txns
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
ORDER BY ym, category;
tasks.hint: Year-month plus category gives 9 groups across the six months.

tasks.prompt: Best month per category by total (RANK over the monthly totals).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, SUM(amount) FROM retail_txns GROUP BY category;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM retail_txns
  GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
)
SELECT ym, category, total
FROM (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total DESC) AS rnk FROM m) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
tasks.hint: One row per category: Outdoor peaks 2026-01 (380), Fitness peaks 2026-03 (140)... verify against the CTE.

tasks.prompt: Rolling 3-month total per category with an explicit window frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, txn_date, amount FROM retail_txns;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM retail_txns
  GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
)
SELECT ym, category,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY ym

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Versioned tables: current state and change history

tasks.prompt: Current state: the latest version of each order (what a MERGE target holds).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, customer, amount, updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY version DESC) AS rn
  FROM delta_orders
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: One row per order_id: o1 through o8.

tasks.prompt: Orders with more than one version: the change-history audit.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, version FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS versions, MAX(version) AS latest_version
FROM delta_orders
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1 (2 versions), o3 (3), o5 (2).

tasks.prompt: Orders whose latest amount differs from their first version: real changes, not no-op rewrites.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, amount, version FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT order_id,
    MIN(CASE WHEN version = 1 THEN amount END) AS first_amt,
    MAX(CASE WHEN version = (SELECT MAX(version) FROM delta_orders d2 WHERE d2.order_id = delta_orders.order_id) THEN amount END) AS last_amt
  FROM delta_orders GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT order_id FROM v WHERE first_amt <> last_amt ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1 (1000 to 1100) and o3 (800 to 900); o5 rewrote the same 1500.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Interview-pressure SQL: CTE chains, frames, ties

tasks.prompt: Three-CTE chain: daily net per account, then account totals, then the top 2 accounts by net flow.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account;

tasks.prompt: 3-day moving average of daily net flow per account, with an explicit ROWS frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) AS net
  FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date
)
SELECT account, txn_date,
  AVG(net) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY txn_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma_3d
FROM daily
ORDER BY account, txn_date;
tasks.hint: Daily grain: a100 has 6 days, a200 has 4, a300 has 4: 14 rows.

tasks.prompt: Top 2 withdrawal amounts per account, keeping ties: DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, amount FROM bank_txns WHERE txn_type = 'withdrawal';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT account, amount
FROM (
  SELECT account, amount,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY ABS(amount) DESC) AS dr
  FROM bank_txns WHERE txn_type = 'withdrawal'
) t
WHERE dr <= 2
ORDER BY account, ABS(amount) DESC;
tasks.hint: a100 keeps both -200 rows (tie for rank 1) plus -120; a200 and a300 contribute one row each.

tasks.prompt: For each account, the day with the largest net outflow; ties broken by earliest date.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) AS net
  FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date
)
SELECT account, txn_date, net
FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY net ASC, txn_date ASC) AS rn
  FROM daily
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY account;

  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS debits,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS credits,

FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
EXCEPT
SELECT account, side, amount, value_date
FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
ORDER BY account;

tasks.prompt: Aging: breaks (either direction) older than 2 days as of 2026-09-05.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM ledger_entries;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH breaks AS (
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  UNION
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
)
SELECT * FROM breaks
WHERE value_date < DATE '2026-09-05' - INTERVAL '2 days'
ORDER BY value_date;
tasks.hint: Only the 2026-08-20 pair for account 1004 is older than 2 days: both its sides.

tasks.prompt: Net break exposure per account: unmatched debits positive, unmatched credits negative; show nonzero.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH breaks AS (
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  UNION
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
)
SELECT account,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) AS net_exposure
FROM breaks
GROUP BY account
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) <> 0
ORDER BY account;
tasks.hint: 1002 nets to -12000 and 1005 to -9000; 1003 and 1004 offset to zero.

tasks.prompt: Completeness: the 3 daily reports across 4 days; find missing report-days.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT DISTINCT report_name FROM report_runs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT SUBSTRING(run_ts, 1, 10) AS day FROM report_runs
),
reps AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT report_name FROM report_runs
  WHERE report_name IN ('CCAR Summary','Liquidity Snapshot','Risk Positions')
),
expected AS (
  SELECT day, report_name FROM days CROSS JOIN reps
)
SELECT e.day, e.report_name
FROM expected e
LEFT JOIN report_runs r
  ON SUBSTRING(r.run_ts, 1, 10) = e.day AND r.report_name = e.report_name
WHERE r.run_id IS NULL;
tasks.hint: Risk Positions never ran on 2026-09-04: the one gap in 12 expected report-days.

tasks.prompt: Checksum changes: runs whose checksum differs from that report's prior run.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum FROM report_runs ORDER BY report_name, run_ts;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum
FROM (
  SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum,
    LAG(checksum) OVER (PARTITION BY report_name ORDER BY run_ts) AS prev_checksum
  FROM report_runs
) t
WHERE prev_checksum IS NOT NULL AND checksum <> prev_checksum
ORDER BY run_ts;
tasks.hint: CCAR Summary on 09-03 and 09-04, and Risk Positions on 09-03: results moved between runs.

tasks.prompt: Four-eyes violations: runs with no approver recorded.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT run_id, report_name, approved_by FROM report_runs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT run_id, report_name, run_ts
FROM report_runs
WHERE approved_by IS NULL
ORDER BY run_ts;
tasks.hint: k3, k8, and k12 ran without a second pair of eyes.

tasks.prompt: Two-proportion z-statistic with pooled standard error; store z in `result`.
tasks.starterCode:
import math
na, nb = 200, 180
xa, xb = 30, 45
result = None
tasks.solutionCode:
import math
na, nb = 200, 180
xa, xb = 30, 45
pa, pb = xa/na, xb/nb
p = (xa + xb) / (na + nb)
se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1/na + 1/nb))
result = (pb - pa) / se

tasks.prompt: With n=200 per arm and baseline 0.15, is a 5-point lift (to 0.20) significant at 95%? Store True/False in `result`.
tasks.solutionCode:
import math
pa, pb, n = 0.15, 0.20, 200
p = (pa + pb) / 2
se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (2 / n))
z = (pb - pa) / se
result = abs(z) > 1.96

checks.description: result is False: z is only about 1.32
